stories.title: The Abbey Theatre
stories.hook: Audiences rioted here in 1907 and 1926.
stories.summary: Audiences rioted here in 1907 and 1926. Poet William Butler Yeats and Lady Gregory founded the Abbey. Englishwoman Annie Horniman paid to convert an old theatre on Abbey Street.
stories.body:
Poet William Butler Yeats and Lady Gregory founded the Abbey. Englishwoman Annie Horniman paid to convert an old theatre on Abbey Street. It opened on 27 December 1904, with plays by Yeats and Lady Gregory.

In 1907, Synge's The Playboy of the Western World caused riots. Much of the rest of the play had to be mimed. In 1925, it became the first state-subsidised theatre in the English-speaking world.

In 1926, O'Casey's The Plough and the Stars sparked another riot. Yeats told the rioters, "You have disgraced yourselves again." In 1951, fire damaged the old theatre. In 1966, a new Abbey opened on the same site, and it still plays there today.

stories.title: Admiral William Brown
stories.hook: A Mayo man founded Argentina's navy.
stories.summary: A Mayo man founded Argentina's navy. William Brown was born in Foxford, Co Mayo, in 1777.
stories.body:
William Brown was born in Foxford, Co Mayo, in 1777. He went to sea young, became a ship's captain, and began trading from Buenos Aires.

In 1814, the government there put him in charge of its fleet. That March, he took Martín García island. Then he beat a Spanish fleet off Montevideo, and the city soon fell.

In 1847, he came back to Ireland and was shocked by the Famine. Argentina has named navy ships, places and streets after him. Every June, Foxford turns blue and white, Argentina's colours, for him.

stories.title: Andrew Jackson's Antrim roots
stories.hook: One Antrim mother's clothes came home without her.
stories.summary: One Antrim mother's clothes came home without her. Elizabeth Jackson left Boneybefore, near Carrickfergus, in 1765.
stories.body:
Elizabeth Jackson left Boneybefore, near Carrickfergus, in 1765. She crossed with her husband and two small sons, to Carolina.

Within two years he died, weeks before her third son, Andrew, was born. Then the Revolution came. Her eldest, Hugh, died after a battle.

Andrew and his brother Robert were captured. She won them back, but Robert died of smallpox. With Andrew well, she went to Charleston to nurse prisoners on British ships.

There she fell ill and died. Her grave was never found. Her clothes came home to Andrew, 14, her hosts' family recalled. He became the seventh US President.

stories.title: Annie Moore & Ellis Island
stories.hook: Ellis Island's first immigrant was a Cork teenager.
stories.summary: Ellis Island's first immigrant was a Cork teenager. Annie Moore sailed from Queenstown, now Cobh, in December 1891 with her two younger brothers.
stories.body:
Annie Moore sailed from Queenstown, now Cobh, in December 1891 with her two younger brothers. On New Year's Day, 1892, Ellis Island opened. Annie was processed first.

She was given a $10 gold piece. Then history lost track of her. For years, the story said she went west to Texas and died in an accident.

That Annie Moore was born in Illinois. In 2006, a genealogist showed who the real Annie was. She stayed on New York's Lower East Side. She had 11 children and buried six. She died in 1924. In 2008, her unmarked grave in Queens finally got a headstone.

stories.title: The Ardagh Chalice
stories.hook: The Sam Maguire Cup copies a chalice from a potato field.
stories.summary: The Sam Maguire Cup copies a chalice from a potato field. In September 1868, two men were digging potatoes in a ringfort near Ardagh.
stories.body:
In September 1868, two men were digging potatoes in a ringfort near Ardagh. Local accounts name Jim Quin and a workman, Paddy Flanagan. A spade struck something hard by a thorn bush.

Under a stone slab lay the chalice. Inside were a bronze cup and four brooches. The original was made in the 8th century, from 354 separate pieces. Apostles' names run around the bowl.

The brooches suggest the hoard was buried around 900. Today it is in the National Museum of Ireland. The first Sam Maguire Cup was presented in 1928. All-Ireland football captains still lift its likeness.

stories.title: The Spanish Armada at Streedagh
stories.hook: Three Armada ships, over 1,000 dead, in Sligo.
stories.summary: Three Armada ships, over 1,000 dead, in Sligo. In September 1588, a storm drove them ashore at Streedagh, County Sligo.
stories.body:
In September 1588, a storm drove them ashore at Streedagh, County Sligo. Captain Francisco de Cuéllar was aboard. He wrote that within an hour, all three broke apart.

He could not swim, he wrote, but four waves threw him ashore on a hatch cover. An English official counted about 1,100 bodies on one Sligo strand. Many who reached the shore were robbed or killed.

Around 1600, a mapmaker drew the three wrecks beside Inishmurray island. Its note reads: three Spanish ships cast away in '88. Gaelic lords sheltered Cuéllar for months. In 1589, safe in Flanders, he wrote it all down.

stories.title: Armagh Observatory
stories.hook: In Armagh, Andromeda became number 224.
stories.summary: In Armagh, Andromeda became number 224. John Dreyer, a young Dane, took charge of Armagh Observatory in 1882.
stories.body:
John Dreyer, a young Dane, took charge of Armagh Observatory in 1882. By then, nebulae were being found faster than the lists could follow.

So Dreyer offered a second supplement. But the Royal Astronomical Society wanted more. The Society asked for one new catalogue to replace all the old lists. Dreyer agreed.

He merged every list and numbered each object in order across the sky. The New General Catalogue was printed in 1888, with 7,840 objects.

Number 224 was the Andromeda nebula, marked most extremely bright. Its description opens with three exclamation marks, the sign for magnificent. Astronomers still use his numbers. Andromeda is still NGC 224.

stories.title: The Siege of Athlone (1691)
stories.hook: Eleven men died in Athlone over some planks.
stories.summary: Eleven men died in Athlone over some planks. In 1691, Williamite troops besieged Athlone, on the Shannon.
stories.body:
In 1691, Williamite troops besieged Athlone, on the Shannon. The Jacobites across the river had broken an arch of the bridge.

So the attackers began laying planks across the gap. A sergeant and ten men in armour came out to tear them down.

A Williamite chaplain, George Story, wrote that all eleven died. Tradition calls the sergeant Custume. Eleven more went out and threw the planks down. Only two escaped.

Two days later, the Williamites waded across the river instead. Behind them, planks bridged the broken arch. Story wrote that Athlone fell in half an hour. The planks crossed after all. Since 1922, Athlone's barracks has borne Custume's name.

stories.title: Bally & Kil: Irish place names
stories.hook: One Irish townland in ten begins with Bally.
stories.summary: One Irish townland in ten begins with Bally. The trail starts with John O'Donovan, a Kilkenny man on the Ordnance Survey.
stories.body:
The trail starts with John O'Donovan, a Kilkenny man on the Ordnance Survey. He travelled most of Ireland, asking old Irish speakers to say the names.

His name books kept each Irish form and his recommended English spelling. P.W. Joyce built his 1869 book of Irish place names on them.

It quotes a count: 6,400 townlands begin with Bally. Bally is baile, a place. Kil is usually cill, a church.

Even O'Donovan's Kilkenny is a Kil: Cill Chainnigh, Canice's church. But Joyce reckoned one Kil in five was coill, a wood. So every Bally and Kil on the map is Irish, in English letters.

stories.title: Balor of Tory Island
stories.hook: Tory's legendary king feared only his grandson.
stories.summary: Tory's legendary king feared only his grandson. An islander told the tale in 1835. Balor of the Evil Eye lived on Tory, off Donegal.
stories.body:
An islander told the tale in 1835. Balor of the Evil Eye lived on Tory, off Donegal. One look from that eye could kill. Then a druid foretold his death at a grandson's hand.

So Balor locked his only daughter, Ethnea, in a tower on Tor Mór. Still, a lover reached her, and she bore three sons. Balor ordered them drowned.

One baby slipped into a bay. A fairy woman carried him safe to his father. Older texts call that boy Lugh. In battle at Mag Tuired, Balor's men raised his eyelid. Then his grandson's sling-stone carried the eye through his head.

stories.title: The banshee
stories.hook: Folklore said the banshee followed O's and Macs.
stories.summary: Folklore said the banshee followed O's and Macs. Yet in Buttevant, Co Cork, she was said to come for a man with neither: rector Charles Bunworth.
stories.body:
Yet in Buttevant, Co Cork, she was said to come for a man with neither: rector Charles Bunworth. He played the Irish harp. Harpers left him 15 harps.

A week before he died, his herdsman came home in tears. He said a white-haired woman had keened beside him. On his last night, the family said, moaning and clapping came at his window. Two men searched and found no footprint.

He died at first light in 1772. His great-grandson, Thomas Crofton Croker, printed the story in 1825. Bean sí means woman of the fairy mound. In folklore, she only foretold the death. She shared the family's grief.

stories.title: The 1796 Bantry Bay expedition
stories.hook: Wolfe Tone came a biscuit's toss from home.
stories.summary: Wolfe Tone came a biscuit's toss from home. In December 1796, a French fleet carried him toward Bantry Bay.
stories.body:
In December 1796, a French fleet carried him toward Bantry Bay. Tone counted 43 ships, carrying General Hoche's army.

But the fleet scattered, and Hoche's frigate went missing. Off the coast, Tone wrote, they came near enough to toss a biscuit ashore.

Then gales blew from the east, day after day. His ship lay six days in the bay, within five hundred yards of shore.

The army never landed. On Christmas night, the order came to put to sea. England, he wrote, had not had such an escape since the Armada. Tone stayed aboard. Ireland stayed a biscuit's toss away.

stories.title: Basking sharks of Achill Island
stories.hook: Irish street lamps once burned shark liver oil.
stories.summary: Irish street lamps once burned shark liver oil. The oil came from basking sharks hunted off Ireland's west coast.
stories.body:
The oil came from basking sharks hunted off Ireland's west coast. This shark is the world's second-largest fish, called the sunfish in Ireland.

Some livers topped a thousand pounds in weight. A naturalist called the oil "fit for lamps." So crews harpooned them, as many as 30 or 40 on a fine day.

Paraffin took over the lamps, but the oil still sold. So by the 1950s, Achill crews were netting them at Keem Bay.

Some seasons, over 1,500 sharks were killed. Then catches fell away. Since 2022, the law protects them. Achill sees them again, and their oil lights no lamps.

stories.title: The Battle of the Boyne (1690)
stories.hook: A Boyne cannonball made France light bonfires.
stories.summary: A Boyne cannonball made France light bonfires. In 1690, King William reached the Boyne, near Drogheda.
stories.body:
In 1690, King William reached the Boyne, near Drogheda. The day before, he rested on the grass near Oldbridge.

Across the river, King James's gunners hid two guns behind a hedge. Their second shot tore his coat and the skin of his shoulder.

A cheer rose across the river. Word spread he was dead. His wound dressed, he rode among his troops that day.

Next morning, his army crossed. King James's army withdrew. The rumour reached France before the truth. A chaplain at the Boyne wrote bonfires were lit for his death. France had lit bonfires for a king who lived.

stories.title: Francis Beaufort & the wind scale
stories.hook: A Meath man put numbers on the wind.
stories.summary: A Meath man put numbers on the wind. Francis Beaufort was born in Navan, County Meath, in 1774. He went to sea at 14.
stories.body:
Francis Beaufort was born in Navan, County Meath, in 1774. He went to sea at 14. By 1806, aboard HMS Woolwich, he was logging wind in numbers, not vague words.

In 1829, the Navy made him Hydrographer, in charge of its charts. He also helped pick Darwin for the Beagle. Each force was judged by how much sail a warship could carry. Force 11 left only storm staysails.

It gave no wind speeds at all. Those were matched to it only in the 1920s. Met Éireann's sea forecasts still use his scale. Gale force 8 is a Navan man's number.

stories.title: The Night of the Big Wind (1839)
stories.hook: In Ireland, one storm could prove your age.
stories.summary: In Ireland, one storm could prove your age. On 6 January 1839, hurricane-force winds swept Ireland. In Irish, Oíche na Gaoithe Móire: the Night of the Big Wind.
stories.body:
On 6 January 1839, hurricane-force winds swept Ireland. In Irish, Oíche na Gaoithe Móire: the Night of the Big Wind. Wind fanned turf fires into thatched roofs. One paper reported over 100 houses burned in Athlone.

In Dublin, a fifth to a quarter of houses were damaged. Ships were wrecked off Donegal and near Liverpool. One study counts about 90 dead in Ireland; others say hundreds.

From 1909, people over 70 could claim a pension; the form came from the post office. State birth registration began only in 1864; many had no written proof. So pension committees asked: do you remember the Big Wind? If you did, you were over 70.

stories.title: The Leviathan of Parsonstown
stories.hook: The world's biggest telescope was in Co Offaly.
stories.summary: The world's biggest telescope was in Co Offaly. In 1845, Lord Rosse finished it at Birr Castle. Its mirror was six feet wide.
stories.body:
In 1845, Lord Rosse finished it at Birr Castle. Its mirror was six feet wide. He built it at Birr with local craftsmen and expert help.

Its tube was over 50 feet long. No larger telescope came for over 70 years. One of its first targets was a faint nebula called M51. He saw spiral arms.

In June 1845, his sketch of the spiral caused a stir among British scientists. He and his team kept refining the drawing. This is a later version. Today we know M51 is a galaxy. Hubble's photo shows the arms he drew at Birr are real.

stories.title: Blarney Castle & the Blarney Stone
stories.hook: The Blarney Stone once stood for tall tales.
stories.summary: The Blarney Stone once stood for tall tales. Blarney Castle, County Cork, was a MacCarthy stronghold. An inscription credits Cormac MacCarthy and the year 1446.
stories.body:
Blarney Castle, County Cork, was a MacCarthy stronghold. An inscription credits Cormac MacCarthy and the year 1446. Tradition says Elizabeth I called a MacCarthy lord's smooth promises Blarney.

A London slang dictionary of 1785 says, "he has licked the Blarney stone." It meant he told tall tales. In 1832, the Dublin Penny Journal said a kiss let you fib without blushing.

An 1896 book says tourists hung by their heels to reach the stone. By 1913, metal grips helped visitors lean back to kiss it. That 1785 dictionary also warned: many claimed the climb who never made it.

stories.title: Bohemians & Dalymount Park
stories.hook: In 1924, America's footballers came to Phibsborough.
stories.summary: In 1924, America's footballers came to Phibsborough. They came to play at Dalymount Park, the home ground of Bohemian FC.
stories.body:
They came to play at Dalymount Park, the home ground of Bohemian FC. On 14 June 1924, the Free State side played its first home match there.

Four of the Free State side were Bohemians. Ned Brooks of Bohs scored all three in a 3-1 win. The club was founded in 1890, in a gate lodge at the Phoenix Park. It opened Dalymount in 1901.

The Irish Times said the visitors were "stones the heavier team". In 2024, the FAI recognised the match as an official international.

stories.title: The Book of Kells
stories.hook: This book is over 1,200 years old.
stories.summary: This book is over 1,200 years old. Around the year 800, monks of a Columban monastery made it. Probably begun on Iona, continued at Kells.
stories.body:
Around the year 800, monks of a Columban monastery made it. Probably begun on Iona, continued at Kells. It holds the four Gospels in Latin, on 340 leaves of calfskin vellum.

In 1007, it was stolen in the night. It turned up months later, under a sod, without its golden cover. Its colours included ochre, copper green and woad.

Look closely, and you'll find a cat and a mouse between the lines. Since 1661, it has lived at Trinity College Dublin. Two pages are on show at a time.

stories.title: George Boole in Cork
stories.hook: Computer logic traces back to a Cork professor.
stories.summary: Computer logic traces back to a Cork professor. George Boole, born in Lincoln, England, came to Cork in 1849.
stories.body:
George Boole, born in Lincoln, England, came to Cork in 1849. He was the first professor of mathematics at Queen's College, now UCC.

In 1854, he published The Laws of Thought. Its title page names his Cork chair. He turned logic into algebra. Its symbols take just two values, 0 and 1.

In the 1930s, engineers applied Boolean algebra to switching circuits. Digital chips are designed with it today. Programmers still call a true-or-false value a Boolean, after him.

stories.title: National Botanic Gardens
stories.hook: Ireland's potato blight was first noted here.
stories.summary: Ireland's potato blight was first noted here. In 1795, the Dublin Society founded these gardens. They were to promote scientific farming.
stories.body:
In 1795, the Dublin Society founded these gardens. They were to promote scientific farming. In 1843, work began on a curvilinear glasshouse. It was mainly the work of Dublin ironmaster Richard Turner.

On 20 August 1845, curator David Moore noted potato blight here. He predicted it would lead to famine. He concluded that a fungus caused it, not the weather. But he never found a remedy.

In 1854, a glasshouse was built for the giant Amazon water lily, the botanical sensation of the time. Turner's curvilinear range was restored in 1995. Today, the gardens are free to enter.

stories.title: Captain Boycott & the word 'boycott'
stories.hook: Boycott was once just a man in Mayo.
stories.summary: Boycott was once just a man in Mayo. He was the land agent at Lough Mask House.
stories.body:
He was the land agent at Lough Mask House. Then, in September 1880, Parnell urged a crowd in Ennis to shun, not shoot.

Days later, Boycott tried to evict tenants, and the shunning fell on him. His workers walked off, leaving his harvest standing in the fields.

So fifty Ulster volunteers, mostly Orangemen, brought it in under armed guard. Saving crops worth a few hundred pounds cost about £10,000.

By then, papers had made his name a verb: to boycott. Soon French, German and Dutch borrowed the word. Boycott the man left Mayo under escort. Boycott the word went round the world.

stories.title: Bram Stoker's Dublin
stories.hook: Dracula's author spent 10 years at Dublin Castle.
stories.summary: Dracula's author spent 10 years at Dublin Castle. Bram Stoker was born in Clontarf in 1847, and was bedridden until age 7.
stories.body:
Bram Stoker was born in Clontarf in 1847, and was bedridden until age 7. He then studied at Trinity College, and excelled as an athlete.

He was a civil servant at Dublin Castle, and reviewed plays for the Dublin Evening Mail. In 1876, he praised Henry Irving's Hamlet. Irving invited him to dinner, and they became friends.

In 1878, Irving offered him a job as business manager of London's Lyceum Theatre. Dracula came out in May 1897. It has never been out of print.

stories.title: Braveheart filmed in Ireland
stories.hook: Braveheart's York was a castle in Co Meath.
stories.summary: Braveheart's York was a castle in Co Meath. In 1994, the film about Scotland's William Wallace was mostly shot in Ireland.
stories.body:
In 1994, the film about Scotland's William Wallace was mostly shot in Ireland. Trim Castle, Co Meath, played the walled city of York.

The battle of Stirling Bridge was filmed on the Curragh, Co Kildare, with no bridge. Hundreds of Irish Army reservists from the FCA played both armies. Scots one day, English the next.

But Trim Castle is no film set. Hugh de Lacy built a wooden castle here in 1172. Hollywood borrowed Trim Castle for one summer. The de Lacys spent decades building Ireland's largest Anglo-Norman castle.

stories.title: The Brazen Head
stories.hook: This Dublin pub claims to be Ireland's oldest.
stories.summary: This Dublin pub claims to be Ireland's oldest. The Brazen Head says it was established in 1198.
stories.body:
The Brazen Head says it was established in 1198. Local tradition says a tavern stood on the site then, but no documents prove it.

It received a licence to sell ale in 1661. The present building went up in 1754, as a coaching inn.

In 1786, a highwayman engraved a message on its staircase window. A 1969 guide says patriots such as Robert Emmet and Wolfe Tone often came here.

stories.title: Brian Boru & the Battle of Clontarf
stories.hook: Irishmen fought on both sides at Clontarf.
stories.summary: Irishmen fought on both sides at Clontarf. Brian Boru is remembered for driving out the Vikings. Around 1005, the Book of Armagh called him Emperor of the Irish.
stories.body:
Brian Boru is remembered for driving out the Vikings. Around 1005, the Book of Armagh called him Emperor of the Irish. Yet he had Viking allies for years. His daughter married Sitric, Dublin's Norse king.

In 1014, Sitric and his uncle, the king of Leinster, led the other side. Vikings from Orkney joined them. Brian's side won, but Brian, by then over seventy, was killed. Early accounts say he was praying in his tent.

Afterwards, Sitric still held Dublin. The Vikings were not driven out. Even Trinity's Brian Boru harp was made centuries after him. Yet it became the model for Ireland's harp emblem.

stories.title: North Bull Island
stories.hook: This 5 km island was an accident.
stories.summary: This 5 km island was an accident. In 1800, Captain Bligh of the Bounty surveyed Dublin Bay. The dry sand here was a tiny patch.
stories.body:
In 1800, Captain Bligh of the Bounty surveyed Dublin Bay. The dry sand here was a tiny patch. The South Wall helped sweep sand northward. By 1818, it was a spit 5 km long.

The North Bull Wall was built from 1820 to 1825. It cost 95,000 pounds. The walls made the tide scour the channel. Much of that sand washed onto the island.

In 1889, the Royal Dublin Golf Club moved onto the island. St Anne's later added a second course. In 1981, UNESCO made it a biosphere reserve. Dollymount Strand runs its whole length.

stories.title: Bunratty Castle
stories.hook: How a Clare castle lost its roof.
stories.summary: How a Clare castle lost its roof. In 1646, the Pope's envoy called Bunratty the most beautiful spot he'd seen.
stories.body:
In 1646, the Pope's envoy called Bunratty the most beautiful spot he'd seen. That spring, William Penn brought Parliament ships up the Shannon.

Penn's account says the Earl of Thomond let his men into the castle. Irish Confederate forces laid siege, and the earl sailed for England.

By July, the garrison gave up the castle. After the earl left, tenants lived in it. Then they built a new house and moved out.

Late in the 1800s, the great hall's roof was let fall. Three centuries after the siege, Lord Gort bought the ruin. He gave it back its roof.

stories.title: The wildflowers of the Burren
stories.hook: Not earth enough to bury a man.
stories.summary: Not earth enough to bury a man. So went a saying about the Burren, in Clare.
stories.body:
So went a saying about the Burren, in Clare. Cromwell's general Edmund Ludlow came in 1651 and wrote down the rest.

Not water enough to drown a man, wood enough to hang one. Yet cattle were fat, he wrote, on sweet grass between the rocks.

In those cracks grow spring gentians, a flower of the Arctic and Alps. Then mountain avens, likely an Ice Age survivor.

Beside them, an orchid of the Mediterranean. The stone holds heat, and Gulf Stream winters stay mild.

Cattle graze there in winter, so spring grass stays short. Not earth enough to bury a man. Just enough for a gentian.

stories.title: Cahir Castle
stories.hook: Cahir's castle on a rock seemed untakeable.
stories.summary: Cahir's castle on a rock seemed untakeable. The rock stands in the River Suir, County Tipperary.
stories.body:
The rock stands in the River Suir, County Tipperary. But in 1599, the Earl of Essex turned heavy guns on it.

The Four Masters say the guns broke down the nearest side. Within a year, Lord Cahir's brother took it back with sixty men and ladders.

Then Cromwell came in 1650. He was told Essex had needed an eight-week siege. So he brought cannon, and sent the governor a letter offering terms.

An account from his army says the governor gave in that same day. Cromwell wrote that the castle on the rock was taken without losing one man.

stories.title: The origins of camogie
stories.hook: Irish women once hid their sticks under coats.
stories.summary: Irish women once hid their sticks under coats. In Dublin, Gaelic League women wanted a hurling game of their own.
stories.body:
In Dublin, Gaelic League women wanted a hurling game of their own. But sport for women was frowned on, the GAA Museum says.

So the sticks went under coats. Still, their stick got a name: camóg, a stick with a crook.

In 1904, two Dublin teams brought their camógs to Navan, County Meath. Keatings played Cúchulainns, in long skirts, in the first public camogie match.

One report noticed the stick: much lighter and less dangerous than the camán. That year, an Irish dictionary filed the game under camóg: a new ladies' game. Nobody hides the stick now. That new ladies' game has over 100,000 members.

stories.title: Carrick-a-Rede Rope Bridge
stories.hook: Antrim's famous rope bridge came down every winter.
stories.summary: Antrim's famous rope bridge came down every winter. Salmon fishermen built it to reach Carrick‑a‑Rede island, near Ballintoy. The National Trust dates the first bridge to 1755.
stories.body:
Salmon fishermen built it to reach Carrick‑a‑Rede island, near Ballintoy. The National Trust dates the first bridge to 1755. In 1784, a visitor gave its name as the rock in the road. The rock sat on the salmon's route home.

He wrote that fishermen put it up each summer, for the salmon. A travel book of 1817 says it was taken down in winter. Rough seas stopped the fishing.

People walked across it, about 100 feet above the water. Below, the sea ran through the gap. The last salmon was caught there in 2002. From 2009, the bridge stayed up all year.

stories.title: Carrickfergus Castle
stories.hook: An American captain came hunting off this castle.
stories.summary: An American captain came hunting off this castle. This is Carrickfergus Castle, County Antrim. John de Courcy began it soon after 1177.
stories.body:
This is Carrickfergus Castle, County Antrim. John de Courcy began it soon after 1177. In 1315, Edward Bruce's Scots laid siege. The castle held out for about a year.

A Dublin annal says the starving guards ate hides, then gave up the castle. On 14 June 1690, William III landed here. His yacht's captain, Greenvile Collins, put it on a sea chart.

A painting from the early 1700s appears to show his barge rowing in. In April 1778, John Paul Jones found HMS Drake at anchor off the town. On 24 April his Ranger came back. After about an hour's fight, the Drake surrendered.

stories.title: Marino's garden temple
stories.hook: This little temple hides 16 rooms.
stories.summary: This little temple hides 16 rooms. Its owner, Lord Charlemont, spent 9 years on a Grand Tour. He came home with a passion for classical architecture.
stories.body:
Its owner, Lord Charlemont, spent 9 years on a Grand Tour. He came home with a passion for classical architecture. In 1759, William Chambers designed him a pleasure house. Chambers sent the plans from London, and never saw it finished.

The 16 rooms are spread over three floors. The basement held the kitchen and a wine cellar. Four of its columns are hollow and hide the drainpipes. The chimneys are disguised as urns.

In the 1800s, its paintings and fireplaces were sold or lost. Large-scale restoration began in 1974. Today, the Office of Public Works cares for it. Visits are by guided tour only.

stories.title: Irish changeling legends
stories.hook: An Irish mother tricked a fairy with eggshells.
stories.summary: An Irish mother tricked a fairy with eggshells. Old tales say fairies stole babies and left look-alikes.
stories.body:
Old tales say fairies stole babies and left look-alikes. In one, a mother in the South of Ireland feared for her baby.

In it, Mrs Sullivan's blue-eyed boy withered overnight. Neighbours said a fairy lay in his place.

So a wise woman, Grey Ellen, set a test. Boil a dozen eggshells, she said, and you'll know.

The child asked Mrs Sullivan, in an old man's voice, what she was doing. Eggshells, she said. He sat up, clapping.

“I'm 1,500 years in the world,” shrieked the imp. His own words gave him away, and he vanished. Her boy lay asleep, and the eggshells had tricked a fairy.

stories.title: Chapelizod & Isolde's Chapel
stories.hook: Chapelizod, tradition says, is Isolde's chapel.
stories.summary: Chapelizod, tradition says, is Isolde's chapel. In the legend, Isolde is an Irish princess. She and the knight Tristan drink a love potion at sea.
stories.body:
In the legend, Isolde is an Irish princess. She and the knight Tristan drink a love potion at sea. In 1577, Richard Stanihurst wrote of a village close to Dublin. He said it was named for la Beale Isoud.

A royal record of 1229 already calls it Capella Isolde. Which Isolde, it never says. Sheridan Le Fanu's 1863 novel The House by the Churchyard is set here.

James Joyce told a friend Finnegans Wake was the story of a Chapelizod family. On its first page, a Sir Tristram comes over the short sea. Scholars hear Tristan, in a book set in Isolde's chapel.

stories.title: Charles Fort, Kinsale
stories.hook: Kinsale's great sea fort fell to a hill.
stories.summary: Kinsale's great sea fort fell to a hill. Charles Fort guarded Kinsale from the sea.
stories.body:
Charles Fort guarded Kinsale from the sea. But its landward side was unfinished. Higher ground looked down into it.

In 1690, after the Boyne, Marlborough's army came overland from Cork. The fort's governor, Edward Scott, refused to surrender.

His reply, in a Williamite history: time enough to talk of that a month hence. So the attackers set their guns on that hill.

For days they pounded the weak eastern wall, until it gave way. After 13 days, about 1,200 defenders, many sick, marched to Limerick. Scott never got his month. His fort faced the sea, and fell to the hill behind it.

stories.title: Charles Thomson & the Great Seal
stories.hook: A County Derry orphan finished the dollar's seal.
stories.summary: A County Derry orphan finished the dollar's seal. Charles Thomson was born in County Derry. His widowed father sailed for America.
stories.body:
Charles Thomson was born in County Derry. His widowed father sailed for America. He died at sea. The children landed in Delaware with nothing.

A blacksmith meant to apprentice Charles. A friend later wrote he ran off at night. He told a woman on the road he wanted to live by his mind and pen.

Later, that pen served Congress, as its Secretary. His name is on the first printed Declaration. In 1782, after three committees had tried, Congress gave him the seal. He and William Barton took a week. Since 1935, both its sides are on the dollar bill.

stories.title: The Children of Lir
stories.hook: Four children. 900 years as swans.
stories.summary: Four children. 900 years as swans. In Irish legend, Lir's four children bathed in Lough Derravaragh, Co Westmeath.
stories.body:
In Irish legend, Lir's four children bathed in Lough Derravaragh, Co Westmeath. Their jealous stepmother, Aoife, turned them into swans with a druid's wand.

Her curse: 300 years there, 300 on the Sea of Moyle, 300 off Erris, Co Mayo. They kept their human voices. Crowds camped by the lake to hear them sing.

On the stormy Moyle, Fionnuala sheltered her brothers from the frost. At last, on Inis Gluaire off Erris, a monk's bell rang.

When the spell broke, they were human again, and very old. Then they died. Fionnuala's last wish: one grave, her brothers around her, just as at sea.

stories.title: The Choctaw famine gift
stories.hook: Why does Midleton have nine giant steel feathers?
stories.summary: Why does Midleton have nine giant steel feathers? In 1847, famine was ravaging Skibbereen in West Cork. Few places suffered worse.
stories.body:
In 1847, famine was ravaging Skibbereen in West Cork. Few places suffered worse. In Indian Territory, now Oklahoma, the Choctaw heard of Ireland's hunger.

About 16 years earlier, the Choctaw were forced from their homeland. Thousands died on the way. Even so, in March 1847, they sent money for Irish famine relief. By most accounts, it was $170.

In 2017, Midleton dedicated Kindred Spirits. Nine steel eagle feathers make the shape of a bowl. In 2020, Irish donors paid it forward to Navajo and Hopi Covid relief. Many named the Choctaw gift.

stories.title: Christ Church Cathedral
stories.hook: This cathedral holds a mummified cat and rat.
stories.summary: This cathedral holds a mummified cat and rat. Christ Church started life as a Viking church, around 1030.
stories.body:
Christ Church started life as a Viking church, around 1030. Its crypt, built from 1172, is one of the largest in Britain or Ireland.

The crypt was later used as a market, and at one stage even a pub. In 1562, the nave roof collapsed and smashed the tomb of Strongbow.

The cat and rat were found years ago, by workers repairing an old organ. In the 1870s, a whiskey distiller paid to rebuild the cathedral into the form it has today.

stories.title: The Claddagh ring
stories.hook: Richard Joyce's Claddagh legend began without a ring.
stories.summary: Richard Joyce's Claddagh legend began without a ring. The legend says Galway's Richard Joyce was enslaved in Algiers and trained as a goldsmith.
stories.body:
The legend says Galway's Richard Joyce was enslaved in Algiers and trained as a goldsmith. Freed after 14 years, the story goes, he came home with a ring for his sweetheart.

But the 1820 account of Joyce never mentions a ring. Only his silver, stamped with his mark. The earliest rings of this style date to about 1700. One bears Joyce's mark, others Thomas Meade's.

The Claddagh was an Irish-speaking fishing village outside Galway's walls, with its own king. Its name only stuck to the ring in the mid-1800s, over a century later. The ring with Joyce's mark is home now, in Galway City Museum.

stories.title: Alcock & Brown's Atlantic landing
stories.hook: The first non-stop Atlantic flight landed in Connemara.
stories.summary: The first non-stop Atlantic flight landed in Connemara. In June 1919, John Alcock and Arthur Brown left Newfoundland. Their plane was a converted bomber.
stories.body:
In June 1919, John Alcock and Arthur Brown left Newfoundland. Their plane was a converted bomber. Alcock flew through fog, snow and sleet. Twice, they nearly hit the sea.

After about 16 hours, they landed near Clifden, Co Galway. Marconi's wireless station was next door. They aimed for what looked like a green field. It was Derrygimlagh bog.

The plane tipped onto its nose, but neither man was hurt. The first reporter there was Tom 'Cork' Kenny of the Connacht Tribune. Next morning, it was world news. Charles Lindbergh flew the Atlantic solo in 1927, eight years later. Connemara got there first.

stories.title: Cliffs of Moher
stories.hook: The Cliffs of Moher began as river mud.
stories.summary: The Cliffs of Moher began as river mud. In County Clare, they run for miles and rise up to 214 metres.
stories.body:
In County Clare, they run for miles and rise up to 214 metres. Over 300 million years ago, rivers carried mud and sand into an ancient sea. Back then, Ireland lay near the equator.

Around 1835, local landlord Cornelius O'Brien built a tower on the cliff top. Today, more than 20,000 seabirds breed here, including puffins and razorbills.

They nest on pale sandstone ledges, between darker bands of shale. A gazetteer of the time said his tower was for visitors. They've been coming to see that old river mud ever since.

stories.title: Clonmacnoise
stories.hook: Lightning beheaded this Offaly round tower in 1135.
stories.summary: Lightning beheaded this Offaly round tower in 1135. St Ciarán founded Clonmacnoise on the Shannon in the 540s. It became a great seat of learning.
stories.body:
St Ciarán founded Clonmacnoise on the Shannon in the 540s. It became a great seat of learning. An etched plan from 1658 names ten churches here, each one a Temple.

The annals say its great belfry was finished in 1124, by a king and an abbot. Eleven years later, the same chronicle recorded the strike. “Lightning knocked off the head of the steeple of Cluain-muc-Nois.”

Raiders came too, Vikings and Irish alike. In 1050, the annals say, it was plundered three times in three months. Its top today is rougher, later stone, likely rebuilt after the strike.

stories.title: Cobh & the Titanic
stories.hook: Some people got off the Titanic in Cork.
stories.summary: Some people got off the Titanic in Cork. On 11 April 1912, she anchored off Roches Point, near Queenstown, now Cobh.
stories.body:
On 11 April 1912, she anchored off Roches Point, near Queenstown, now Cobh. Two tenders, the America and the Ireland, ferried passengers out to her.

Cobh Heritage Centre counts 123 who boarded, most in third class. A handful of passengers left her there, among them Francis Browne, a Jesuit with a camera.

So did a Queenstown stoker, John Coffey, who deserted the ship. That afternoon she sailed for New York. On 15 April, she sank, and about 1,500 people died. Three years later, Queenstown took in the Lusitania's survivors, and buried many of her dead.

stories.title: Cork City FC
stories.hook: For two seasons, Cork had no league club.
stories.summary: For two seasons, Cork had no league club. Cork's League of Ireland football had begun with Ford's factory on the Marina.
stories.body:
Cork's League of Ireland football had begun with Ford's factory on the Marina. The works team, Fordsons, even won the FAI Cup.

But Ford cut the club loose. Within a decade, it was wound up. Club after club followed, won trophies, then ran out of money.

Even Cork United, with five league titles, went into liquidation. When a second Cork United was expelled, nobody took its place.

Then in 1984, the year Ford's Cork plant closed, Cork City was formed. Cork has not gone a season without a league club since.

stories.title: Croagh Patrick
stories.hook: Some climb this Mayo mountain barefoot every July.
stories.summary: Some climb this Mayo mountain barefoot every July. Croagh Patrick rises about 765 metres above Clew Bay, near Westport. Locals call it the Reek.
stories.body:
Croagh Patrick rises about 765 metres above Clew Bay, near Westport. Locals call it the Reek. In the 7th century, Tírechán wrote that Patrick spent 40 days on its summit. Tradition says it was 441.

A later Life of Patrick says black birds filled the mountain. He struck his bell at them. Reek Sunday is the last Sunday of July. Thousands climb, and Masses are said on top.

The summit chapel dates from 1905. Digs near it found an older stone oratory, dated AD 430 to 890. A stone rampart also rings the whole summit. Archaeologists list the site as a hillfort.

stories.title: Croke Park
stories.hook: Ireland's biggest stadium was bought for 3,500 pounds.
stories.summary: Ireland's biggest stadium was bought for 3,500 pounds. In 1913, the GAA bought the old City and Suburban Racecourse. They renamed it after their first patron, Archbishop Thomas Croke.
stories.body:
In 1913, the GAA bought the old City and Suburban Racecourse. They renamed it after their first patron, Archbishop Thomas Croke. On 21 November 1920, Dublin played Tipperary here at Gaelic football. Crown forces raided the ground and opened fire on the crowd.

Fourteen people lost their lives, including Michael Hogan, a Tipperary player. The stand built here in 1924 was named the Hogan Stand, in his memory.

In 2007, England played rugby here. Irish fans stood silent for England's anthem. Today it holds 82,300 people, one of Europe's largest stadiums.

stories.title: The theft of the Irish Crown Jewels
stories.hook: Ireland's crown jewels vanished in 1907. Never found.
stories.summary: Ireland's crown jewels vanished in 1907. Never found. The jewels included no crown. They were a diamond star and badges, in a safe at Dublin Castle.
stories.body:
The jewels included no crown. They were a diamond star and badges, in a safe at Dublin Castle. On 6 July 1907, days before a royal visit, the safe was found unlocked. The jewels were gone.

Sir Arthur Vicars, Ulster King of Arms, held both safe keys. The lock was not forced. A 1908 inquiry blamed his lack of care. He was dismissed, and called himself a scapegoat.

Some historians suspect Francis Shackleton, his herald and the explorer Ernest's brother. Police found no evidence against him. No one was ever charged. One historian thinks the jewels were broken up long ago, perhaps into rings.

stories.title: The Custom House
stories.hook: The Custom House burned for 5 days.
stories.summary: The Custom House burned for 5 days. In 1781, John Beresford made James Gandon its architect.
stories.body:
In 1781, John Beresford made James Gandon its architect. Some city merchants complained it was being built on what was then a swamp.

It opened in 1791, at a cost of 200,000 pounds. On 25 May 1921, the Irish Republican Army burned it, to disrupt British rule by destroying tax records.

Gandon's interior was destroyed, the dome collapsed, and centuries of records were lost. The Irish Free State restored it, rebuilding the dome in a darker Irish limestone.

stories.title: Derry City FC
stories.hook: Derry City joined a league across the border.
stories.summary: Derry City joined a league across the border. Founded in 1928, the club made the Brandywell its home.
stories.body:
Founded in 1928, the club made the Brandywell its home. In 1965, it won the Irish League, Northern Ireland's top division.

In 1971, during the Troubles, home games moved 30 miles to Coleraine. In 1972, after losing a vote to return home, it withdrew. After 13 years in junior football, it joined the League of Ireland in 1985. Its ground is a few miles from the border.

In 1989, a packed Brandywell saw Derry City win the league. With the League Cup and FAI Cup, it was a treble. RTÉ called them the first league champions on both sides of the border.

stories.title: The walls of Derry
stories.hook: Derry's walls were never breached. Something else was.
stories.summary: Derry's walls were never breached. Something else was. London's Irish Society began them in 1613. They guarded settlers from England and Scotland.
stories.body:
London's Irish Society began them in 1613. They guarded settlers from England and Scotland. Seventy-five years on, apprentices shut the gates on King James's troops.

By April 1689, his army had the city surrounded. Shells fell for weeks, but the walls held.

The danger was a boom chained across the Foyle, to stop ships bringing food. Inside, people starved, and accounts say thousands died.

Three months in, relief ships broke the boom. The Mountjoy's master, Michael Browning, was shot dead.

Food got through, and within days the besieging army left. The walls were never breached. The boom on the Foyle was.

stories.title: Diarmuid & Gráinne's beds
stories.hook: Many Irish stone tombs are called lovers' beds.
stories.summary: Many Irish stone tombs are called lovers' beds. In Clare, map-makers marked such dolmens Diarmuid and Gráinne's Bed.
stories.body:
In Clare, map-makers marked such dolmens Diarmuid and Gráinne's Bed. In the tale, Gráinne was promised to Fionn mac Cumhaill, older than her father.

She fled with his warrior Diarmuid. Each night, tradition says, they slept in a new dolmen. A year and a day's running would mean 366 beds.

Years later, a boar gored Diarmuid on Ben Bulben in Sligo. Water from Fionn's hands could heal him. Twice, Fionn let it slip.

The third time, he brought it. Diarmuid died as it reached him. But Ireland's oldest dolmens go back 5,000 years. So the beds are far older than the tale.

stories.title: Dublin Castle
stories.hook: Britain governed Ireland from this castle until 1922.
stories.summary: Britain governed Ireland from this castle until 1922. King John of England ordered it built in 1204, as a major defensive work.
stories.body:
King John of England ordered it built in 1204, as a major defensive work. It was built beside the dark pool that gave Dublin its name.

Its Record Tower, from about 1228, is the only tower left from the original castle. After a severe fire in 1684, rebuilding turned the medieval fortress into a Georgian palace.

On 16 January 1922, it was handed over to Michael Collins and the new Provisional Government. Today, it hosts the inauguration of every President of Ireland.

stories.title: The 1913 Dublin Lockout
stories.hook: In 1913, Larkin spoke from his rival's hotel.
stories.summary: In 1913, Larkin spoke from his rival's hotel. From August 1913, employers led by William Martin Murphy sacked Larkin's union members. About 20,000 ended up on strike or locked out.
stories.body:
From August 1913, employers led by William Martin Murphy sacked Larkin's union members. About 20,000 ended up on strike or locked out. Larkin's meeting on Sackville Street was banned. On 31 August, he spoke from a balcony of Murphy's Imperial Hotel.

Police baton-charged the crowd. It became known as Bloody Sunday. Hundreds were hurt that weekend, and at least two men died. On 27 September, the ship Hare brought 60,000 food parcels from British trade unionists.

By early 1914, hungry workers were returning. Many signed a pledge never to join the union. Today, a 1960s tower stands on the old Liberty Hall site. It is still a union headquarters.

stories.title: Dublin Mean Time
stories.hook: Irish clocks once ran 25 minutes behind Britain.
stories.summary: Irish clocks once ran 25 minutes behind Britain. Their time was set at Dunsink Observatory, founded outside Dublin in 1785.
stories.body:
Their time was set at Dunsink Observatory, founded outside Dublin in 1785. In 1827, William Rowan Hamilton became Royal Astronomer of Ireland. He was 21.

In 1880, a new law made Dunsink's local time Ireland's legal time. Called Dublin Mean Time, it ran 25 minutes and 21 seconds behind Greenwich.

On 1 October 1916, months after the Rising, Ireland switched to Greenwich time. Dunsink still stands, and its 1868 telescope now hosts public stargazing nights.

stories.title: Dublin's trams & the Luas
stories.hook: Dublin scrapped its trams, then brought them back.
stories.summary: Dublin scrapped its trams, then brought them back. In 1872, horse trams began running to Terenure.
stories.body:
In 1872, horse trams began running to Terenure. Routes ran from Nelson's Pillar to Drumcondra, Terenure and even Howth.

In 1896, Dublin's first electric trams ran to Dalkey. By 1901, the whole city system was electric.

In 1904, it was called one of the world's most impressive. The last city route, to Dalkey, closed in July 1949. Souvenir hunters damaged its last tram, despite 60 guards. In 2004, trams returned as the Luas. Luas is Irish for speed.

stories.title: Dublin Zoo
stories.hook: A movie-star lion may have been born here.
stories.summary: A movie-star lion may have been born here. Dublin Zoo opened in the Phoenix Park in September 1831.
stories.body:
Dublin Zoo opened in the Phoenix Park in September 1831. Unlike London Zoo, it welcomed everybody, not just members.

Its first lions came in 1855. From 1857 to 1876, 92 cubs were born here. Even former American president Ulysses Grant came to see Dublin's lions.

Reports suggest Slats, the first MGM lion, was born here in 1919. In 1838, Queen Victoria's coronation open day drew 20,000 people. That is still its one-day record.

stories.title: The dullahan
stories.hook: Ireland's headless rider carries his own head.
stories.summary: Ireland's headless rider carries his own head. Folklore calls him the Dullahan. Thomas Crofton Croker printed tales of him in 1828.
stories.body:
Folklore calls him the Dullahan. Thomas Crofton Croker printed tales of him in 1828. In one, Charley Culnane rides home by the Blackwater. A giant on a headless white horse joins him.

Charley sees no head. A voice under the rider's arm says, “Look again, Charley Culnane.” The head looks like a cream cheese hung with black puddings. He says he broke his neck at Kilcummer hill a century ago.

Croker also heard of a headless coach near Ballyhooly. People took it as a sign of death. In Doneraile, people said it stopped at doors on Saturday nights. Whoever opened up got a basin of blood in the face.

stories.title: Dún Aonghasa
stories.hook: This Aran fort's walls stop at a cliff.
stories.summary: This Aran fort's walls stop at a cliff. Dún Aonghasa, on Inis Mór in Galway, sits above an 87-metre drop.
stories.body:
Dún Aonghasa, on Inis Mór in Galway, sits above an 87-metre drop. Three curving drystone walls guard the land side. The cliff guards the rest.

Between the walls, thousands of jagged stones stand on end to slow attackers. It's a chevaux-de-frise. Digs in the 1990s dated its first walls to about 1100 BC. Clay moulds show swords and spearheads were cast here.

Medieval lore names it for Aonghus of the Fir Bolg. His people, it says, fled a crushing rent owed to Tara. That tale is set about 2,000 years ago. By then its first walls were about a thousand years old.

stories.title: Dún Laoghaire Harbour
stories.hook: Ireland's first passenger railway ran to this harbour.
stories.summary: Ireland's first passenger railway ran to this harbour. In 1807, two troopships were wrecked nearby. Over 400 lives were lost.
stories.body:
In 1807, two troopships were wrecked nearby. Over 400 lives were lost. The disaster boosted calls for a refuge harbour. Work began in 1817.

King George the Fourth sailed from here in 1821. The town was renamed Kingstown in his honour. The line from Dublin opened in December 1834. Almost 5,000 paying passengers rode on the first day.

Building the harbour took 42 years. Its piers used granite from nearby Dalkey. In 1920, the town took back its Irish name, Dún Laoghaire.

stories.title: Dundalk FC
stories.hook: Dundalk FC began as a railway rugby team.
stories.summary: Dundalk FC began as a railway rugby team. The Great Northern Railway had its works in Dundalk, County Louth.
stories.body:
The Great Northern Railway had its works in Dundalk, County Louth. Its workers had a rugby club. In 1903, they switched to a round ball.

Locals called them the Railwaymen, in GNR black and amber. They climbed out of junior football, and in 1926 joined the Free State League.

The next year, they swapped the railway's colours for white shirts. Then the members dropped G.N.R. from the club's name. It was simply Dundalk. Within a few seasons, the club these railwaymen built won the league. The old railway rugby team were the first champions outside Dublin.

stories.title: Dunguaire Castle
stories.hook: A Galway king was remembered for one hand.
stories.summary: A Galway king was remembered for one hand. Guaire's fort, tradition says, stood at Kinvara.
stories.body:
Guaire's fort, tradition says, stood at Kinvara. A high king defeated him.

Keating says Guaire knelt, the victor's sword point in his teeth. To test his famous giving, the victor sent a leper to beg.

Guaire gave his gold pin, then his belt. The victor's men took both. Guaire wept, not for himself but for God's poor one.

So the victor made peace. The tale says his hand for the poor was longer than his hand for the bards.

Tradition says his descendants built a tower on his fort in 1520. Its name is still his: Dún Guaire, the king with the longer hand.

stories.title: John Boyd Dunlop in Belfast
stories.hook: Air tyres were invented twice, once in Belfast.
stories.summary: Air tyres were invented twice, once in Belfast. In 1887, young Johnnie Dunlop complained of bumpy rides on Belfast's cobbles.
stories.body:
In 1887, young Johnnie Dunlop complained of bumpy rides on Belfast's cobbles. His father, vet John Boyd Dunlop, gave the boy's tricycle air-filled tyres. He patented the tyre in 1888.

In May 1889, Willie Hume raced on them at the Queen's College sports. He won all four events. In 1890, Dunlop learned his patent was invalid. Robert William Thomson had patented air tyres in 1845.

His "aerial wheels" ran on horse carriages. Rubber cost too much, and the idea lay unused for about 40 years. So Belfast wasn't first with the idea. But a boy's tricycle there is where air tyres finally took off.

stories.title: Dunluce Castle
stories.hook: A lost town lies buried beside Dunluce Castle.
stories.summary: A lost town lies buried beside Dunluce Castle. In 1513, the MacQuillans held this County Antrim cliff castle. The MacDonnells seized it in the 1550s.
stories.body:
In 1513, the MacQuillans held this County Antrim cliff castle. The MacDonnells seized it in the 1550s. In 1588, Armada ships were wrecked nearby. Sorley Boy MacDonnell kept a Spanish gun.

In 1590, a MacQuillan still claimed Dunluce. His letter says the gun stood on the castle. A famous tale says the kitchens fell into the sea in 1639.

A guide quoted in 1832 put it sixty or eighty years before. Randal, Sorley Boy's son, laid out a town here in 1608. It was burned in the 1641 rising. In 2008, archaeologists found it under a field. One merchant's house had an indoor privy.

stories.title: Elizabeth O'Farrell
stories.hook: Her boots were painted out of this photo.
stories.summary: Her boots were painted out of this photo. Dublin, 29 April 1916. Elizabeth O'Farrell of Cumann na mBan walked up Moore Street with a white flag.
stories.body:
Dublin, 29 April 1916. Elizabeth O'Farrell of Cumann na mBan walked up Moore Street with a white flag. Under fire, she carried messages to the British. Then she walked beside Pearse as he surrendered.

She took Pearse's surrender order to the Four Courts, Jacob's and Boland's Mill. The photo shows only her skirt and boots. She later said she stepped back on purpose, and regretted it.

One printed version painted out even her boots. One historian says it was London's Daily Sketch. She spent the rest of her working life as a Holles Street midwife. The park on City Quay where she was born now bears her name.

stories.title: Ireland's Eurovision dynasty
stories.hook: Only one country won Eurovision three times running.
stories.summary: Only one country won Eurovision three times running. It's Ireland, with seven wins, a record now shared with Sweden. The first was Dana's, in Amsterdam in 1970.
stories.body:
It's Ireland, with seven wins, a record now shared with Sweden. The first was Dana's, in Amsterdam in 1970. In 1980, Johnny Logan won.

In 1987 he won again, the first performer to win twice. Then he wrote the 1992 winner for Linda Martin.

In 1993, Niamh Kavanagh won in Millstreet, County Cork. In 1994, the contest came to the Point in Dublin. Paul Harrington and Charlie McGettigan made it three in a row. No other country has done it.

That night's interval act lasted seven minutes. It was Riverdance, and it went on to tour six continents.

stories.title: Irish fairy forts
stories.hook: Irish farmers would not plough these earthen rings.
stories.summary: Irish farmers would not plough these earthen rings. Folklore called them fairy forts.
stories.body:
Folklore called them fairy forts. In a tale Lady Wilde printed, a farmer built a barn on a fairy fort.

He was struck senseless. A voice said, “Pull down the barn, for ill-luck is on it.” So the barn came down. William Carleton wrote nobody dared cut the thorns on a fort.

The forts stayed, and mapmakers marked them Fort. Archaeologists say they were farmsteads, ringed by bank and ditch.

Tens of thousands survive, Ireland's most common ancient monument. The fairy fort was a farmer's home. Scholars say fear helped keep the plough off these rings.

stories.title: Fastnet Rock Lighthouse
stories.hook: They call Cork's Fastnet Rock Ireland's Teardrop.
stories.summary: They call Cork's Fastnet Rock Ireland's Teardrop. It is said many emigrants saw it as their last sight of Ireland.
stories.body:
It is said many emigrants saw it as their last sight of Ireland. In 1854, a cast-iron lighthouse was lit on its summit. It soon proved too weak.

The sea threw a block of up to three tons off the cliff. Cups flew off a table inside. A granite tower was built on a lower ledge. Its blocks were cut in Cornwall and dovetailed together.

Foreman James Kavanagh set all 2,074 blocks. He died in 1903, before the new light was lit. The new light shone on 27 June 1904. For ships from America, it was often the first light of Ireland.

stories.title: The first All-Ireland final (1888)
stories.hook: Hurling's first All-Ireland field is now a supermarket.
stories.summary: Hurling's first All-Ireland field is now a supermarket. That field lay in Birr, then Parsonstown, in King's County, now Offaly.
stories.body:
That field lay in Birr, then Parsonstown, in King's County, now Offaly. Thurles came there to play Meelick on Easter Sunday, 1888.

Each club played for its county, Tipperary against Galway. But seven Thurles regulars refused to play, in a row over expenses.

So Jim Stapleton captained the side. That afternoon, forty-two hurlers marched through Birr. They carried hurleys like rifles.

Across the Camcor river, they reached a field beside the railway station. Thousands watched Thurles win. Meelick never scored.

The papers said Stapleton was carried shoulder-high through the field. Shoppers cross that field now, past a sixteen-foot bronze hurler.

stories.title: The Flight of the Earls
stories.hook: One ship took Ulster's earls away for good.
stories.summary: One ship took Ulster's earls away for good. In September 1607, a French ship lay at anchor in Lough Swilly, Donegal.
stories.body:
In September 1607, a French ship lay at anchor in Lough Swilly, Donegal. At midday, the earls Hugh O'Neill and Rory O'Donnell went aboard at Rathmullan.

Tadhg Ó Cianáin, on board, recorded ninety-nine people on that ship. The Four Masters wrote no ship from Ireland in their time bore nobler men.

But neither earl saw Ireland again. Rory O'Donnell died in Rome the next summer. Hugh O'Neill died there in 1616. Both lie in the same church.

Back in Ulster, the Crown took their lands for English and Scottish settlers. That one ship had opened the way for the Plantation of Ulster.

stories.title: The Seven Wonders of Fore
stories.hook: Westmeath locals say a saint lifted this stone.
stories.summary: Westmeath locals say a saint lifted this stone. Sir Henry Piers saw the stone over St Féchín's church door in Fore.
stories.body:
Sir Henry Piers saw the stone over St Féchín's church door in Fore. One stone, about six feet long. He had seen none bigger so high.

He guessed builders had machines. A local man smiled: the saint did it alone. The workmen could not raise it, so they went to breakfast.

Féchín stayed, he said, and when they came back, the stone was in place. Piers wrote it down in 1682, doubting the miracle.

But hands alone, he wrote, could never have raised that stone. Fore counts it among its Seven Wonders. Whoever lifted the stone, it is still there.

stories.title: The Four Courts
stories.hook: Ireland's Civil War began at this building.
stories.summary: Ireland's Civil War began at this building. James Gandon designed its dome and Round Hall. The foundation stone was laid in 1786.
stories.body:
James Gandon designed its dome and Round Hall. The foundation stone was laid in 1786. In April 1922, anti-Treaty forces occupied the building.

On 28 June, after an unanswered ultimatum, the National Army opened fire. On 30 June, an explosion and fire destroyed much of the Public Record Office. Hundreds of thousands of documents were lost.

Restorers found the dome's columns were carved on all sides. They turned the damaged faces inward. Today, a Virtual Record Treasury rebuilds the lost archive online, using records from 70 archives.

stories.title: Francis Rynd's hollow needle
stories.hook: A Dublin surgeon's needle had no plunger.
stories.summary: A Dublin surgeon's needle had no plunger. In 1844, Margaret Cox came to the Meath Hospital in agonising face pain.
stories.body:
In 1844, Margaret Cox came to the Meath Hospital in agonising face pain. Surgeon Francis Rynd let morphia under her skin, through a hollow needle.

Fluid was dropped into the needle from a writing pen, and simply ran down. Within a minute, his report said, her pain was gone. She slept better that night.

Within ten years, Alexander Wood in Edinburgh added a plunger. Wood usually gets the credit. Rynd's drawing of his needle appeared in 1861.

The same issue carried his obituary. He had died suddenly days before. Yet his Dublin case is often called the first recorded injection. No plunger needed.

stories.title: Gallarus Oratory
stories.hook: Historians still can't date this rain-shedding church.
stories.summary: Historians still can't date this rain-shedding church. Gallarus Oratory overlooks Smerwick Harbour, on the Dingle peninsula.
stories.body:
Gallarus Oratory overlooks Smerwick Harbour, on the Dingle peninsula. Charles Smith described it in 1756. Inside, he wrote, a knife point could hardly pass between its stones.

He wrote that a cell of the same kind admits no rain through its roof. Nearly a century later, George Petrie printed its picture. He thought it might predate Saint Patrick's mission.

But in 1970, Peter Harbison argued it could be as late as the twelfth century. Even he called that case speculative. The date is still an open question. Whatever its age, its stones slope down and outward. So the rain runs off.

stories.title: The Galway to Clifden Railway
stories.hook: Connemara had a railway for just 40 years.
stories.summary: Connemara had a railway for just 40 years. From 1889, new laws paid for light railways in poor, remote districts. They were often called Balfour lines, after the Chief Secretary.
stories.body:
From 1889, new laws paid for light railways in poor, remote districts. They were often called Balfour lines, after the Chief Secretary. The Connemara line left Galway on a steel viaduct over the Corrib. Its three main spans were each 150 feet long.

It opened in 1895, running west by Recess and Ballynahinch to Clifden. Visitors came on the Connemara express from Dublin. The railway company built a hotel for them at Recess.

But freight stayed thin, and road traffic grew. The last train left Clifden on 27 April 1935. The viaduct's stone piers still stand in the Corrib. Parts of the route are now the Connemara Greenway.

stories.title: General Post Office (GPO)
stories.hook: The Easter Rising's headquarters was a post office.
stories.summary: The Easter Rising's headquarters was a post office. The General Post Office opened on 6 January 1818.
stories.body:
The General Post Office opened on 6 January 1818. Its portico has 6 fluted Ionic columns, topped by 3 statues by John Smyth.

On Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, the Rising's leaders occupied it. Outside it, Patrick Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic.

After days of shelling, fire spread to the building. Only its granite facade survived. It was not rebuilt until 1929, by the Irish Free State government. It remains Dublin's principal post office.

stories.title: Giant's Causeway
stories.hook: Legend says an Irish giant built this.
stories.summary: Legend says an Irish giant built this. This is the Giant's Causeway, Co Antrim. Fionn mac Cumhaill built it to fight a Scottish giant, Benandonner.
stories.body:
This is the Giant's Causeway, Co Antrim. Fionn mac Cumhaill built it to fight a Scottish giant, Benandonner. Fionn saw Benandonner was far bigger. In one telling, his wife Oonagh dressed him as a baby.

If that was the baby, how big was the father? Benandonner fled, tearing up the causeway. Science has another story. Some 50 to 60 million years ago, lava cooled and cracked here.

That made about 40,000 basalt columns. In 1986, UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site. Across the sea, Staffa in Scotland has matching columns at Fingal's Cave. And Fingal is an 18th-century poet's version of Fionn.

stories.title: Glasnevin Cemetery
stories.hook: Watchtowers once guarded these graves from body snatchers.
stories.summary: Watchtowers once guarded these graves from body snatchers. In 1823, a priest was stopped from praying at a Catholic funeral. Daniel O'Connell pushed for a new burial ground.
stories.body:
In 1823, a priest was stopped from praying at a Catholic funeral. Daniel O'Connell pushed for a new burial ground. His cemetery, for all religions and none, opened in 1832. The first burial was an 11-year-old boy.

Medical schools needed bodies, and Dublin was a centre of body snatching. At night, bloodhounds roamed the cemetery. O'Connell died in 1847. His heart was buried in Rome, and his body here.

In 1869, his remains were moved to a crypt beneath Ireland's tallest round tower. Today, almost 1.5 million people rest here. Its museum and tower are open to visitors.

stories.title: Glendalough
stories.hook: Walter Scott, lame, crawled into St Kevin's Bed.
stories.summary: Walter Scott, lame, crawled into St Kevin's Bed. At Glendalough, County Wicklow, St Kevin founded a monastery in the 500s.
stories.body:
At Glendalough, County Wicklow, St Kevin founded a monastery in the 500s. St Kevin's Bed is a cliff cave above the Upper Lake. The story goes he lived and prayed there.

In 1825, Scott crawled along the cliff to it. His son-in-law wrote: “the first lame man that ever tried it.” Pilgrims still came to the ruins. An 1834 print shows the round tower without its cap.

Its cap was rebuilt in 1876 from the original stones. The tower stands about 30 metres. Told he was a poet, Scott's guide was indignant. No poet, she said: a gentleman who gave her half-a-crown.

stories.title: Glenveagh Castle
stories.hook: This valley held 244 people before its castle.
stories.summary: This valley held 244 people before its castle. They were tenants of Derryveagh, in County Donegal.
stories.body:
They were tenants of Derryveagh, in County Donegal. Their landlord was land speculator John George Adair.

Then, in April 1861, he had them evicted. Over three days, their homes were levelled.

Among the evicted were 159 children. A reporter wrote that one old man kissed his doorposts.

On the road, one writer said, some pulled grass from family graves. Many sailed for Australia. Others ended up in the workhouse.

Years later, Adair built his castle on Lough Veagh. Its last private owner, from Philadelphia, gave it to the nation. The valley that held 244 is now a national park, open to all.

stories.title: The 1903 Gordon Bennett Cup
stories.hook: British racing green may have begun at a Kildare motor race.
stories.summary: British racing green may have begun at a Kildare motor race. On 2 July 1903, roads in Kildare, Laois and Carlow closed for the race.
stories.body:
On 2 July 1903, roads in Kildare, Laois and Carlow closed for the race. A British car won the Gordon Bennett Cup in 1902, so Britain had to host. But road racing there was illegal.

Ireland was then in the UK, so Parliament passed a law for Ireland only. Councils could now close public roads for races. Belgian Camille Jenatzy won for Germany in a Mercedes. It took him 6 hours 39 minutes.

Each nation had its own colour. A Kildare paper said England's cars would be green, in compliment to Ireland. The winning Napier of 1902 was already green. Still, many say British racing green began here.

stories.title: Grace Gifford & Kilmainham Gaol
stories.hook: They married in Kilmainham, hours before his execution.
stories.summary: They married in Kilmainham, hours before his execution. Grace Gifford was a Dublin artist and cartoonist. In 1915, she got engaged to the poet Joseph Plunkett.
stories.body:
Grace Gifford was a Dublin artist and cartoonist. In 1915, she got engaged to the poet Joseph Plunkett. A leader of the Easter Rising, he was sentenced to death.

On 3 May 1916, they married in the prison chapel. His handcuffs came off only for the ceremony. That night, she was brought back to say goodbye. A guard, watch in hand, said: “Ten minutes.”

He was executed the next morning. That June, she signed this drawing of him as Grace Plunkett. She went on to publish books of cartoons. In 1985, Frank and Seán O’Meara wrote a song about her, called Grace.

stories.title: Grace O'Malley, the Pirate Queen
stories.hook: A Mayo woman sea captain met Queen Elizabeth.
stories.summary: A Mayo woman sea captain met Queen Elizabeth. Gráinne Mhaol, or Grace O'Malley, commanded galleys off Co Mayo. Sir Henry Sidney called her a famous feminine sea captain.
stories.body:
Gráinne Mhaol, or Grace O'Malley, commanded galleys off Co Mayo. Sir Henry Sidney called her a famous feminine sea captain. In 1593, she petitioned the Queen against Richard Bingham, governor of Connacht.

Lord Burghley replied with 18 written questions. In one answer, she says Bingham had gallows made for her. Bingham also jailed her son Tibbot. She took her case to London.

In September 1593, she met the Queen at Greenwich. Tibbot was later freed. Later tales made them equals, two queens. The records show a petitioner at court. In 1627, that son, Tibbot, became the first Viscount Mayo.

stories.title: Dublin's Grand Canal
stories.hook: Part of Dublin's Luas follows a filled-in canal.
stories.summary: Part of Dublin's Luas follows a filled-in canal. Work began in 1756 on a canal to the River Shannon. It took until 1804 to open.
stories.body:
Work began in 1756 on a canal to the River Shannon. It took until 1804 to open. In 1780, passenger boats began running between Dublin and Sallins.

In 1796, docks opened at Ringsend, where the canal meets the Liffey. Two of their locks were built for ocean-going ships. In 1807, a hotel for canal passengers opened at Portobello Harbour.

In 1974, the canal harbour at James's Street closed. The Red Line Luas now follows much of the old line. Since 1991, a statue of poet Patrick Kavanagh has sat on a canal bench. Today, its tree-lined banks are a favourite with cyclists and walkers.

stories.title: Great Blasket Island
stories.hook: A Kerry islander wrote his island's last line.
stories.summary: A Kerry islander wrote his island's last line. Tomás Ó Criomhthain fished from the Great Blasket, off Dún Chaoin.
stories.body:
Tomás Ó Criomhthain fished from the Great Blasket, off Dún Chaoin. Scholars came to learn his Irish. One urged him to write his life.

He did, so that some record of his people might live. An tOileánach was published in 1929.

But in January 1947, a storm cut the island off. Seáinín Ó Cearna lay ill there with meningitis.

No doctor could cross, and he died. His brother called it the end of the island. Within seven years, the state moved most of those left to Dún Chaoin. Tomás had already written their last line: the like of us will never be again.

stories.title: Grianán of Aileach
stories.hook: A king tried carrying a Donegal fort home.
stories.summary: A king tried carrying a Donegal fort home. The Grianán of Aileach, above Inishowen, seated the northern kings.
stories.body:
The Grianán of Aileach, above Inishowen, seated the northern kings. In 1101, the King of Munster tore it down, to avenge his ruined Kincora.

The annals say he had a stone carried south for every sack of food. A verse mocked it: the stones of Aileach, billeted on his horses.

For centuries, the fort crumbled into a heap of fallen stone. Then a doctor in Derry, Walter Bernard, set farmers to rebuild it.

Bernard doubted many stones ever left. His men laughed at the tale. They had too many stones on their farms already. By 1878 it stood again, rebuilt from stones that had stayed home.

stories.title: Guinness's 9,000-year lease
stories.hook: Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease.
stories.summary: Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease. 31 December 1759. Arthur Guinness leases an unused brewery at St James's Gate.
stories.body:
31 December 1759. Arthur Guinness leases an unused brewery at St James's Gate. Forty-five pounds a year. For 9,000 years.

By 1886, it was the largest brewery in the world. Horses hauled the casks. From the 1870s, it also had its own railway. And the lease? It no longer applies. Guinness bought the land outright.

stories.title: The Hag of Beara
stories.hook: Beara's stone woman watches the tide, and speaks.
stories.summary: Beara's stone woman watches the tide, and speaks. Tradition calls her the Cailleach Bhéarra, the Hag of Beara.
stories.body:
Tradition calls her the Cailleach Bhéarra, the Hag of Beara. Her stone stands at Kilcatherine, near Eyeries, facing Coulagh Bay.

One telling says she waits for her husband, Manannán, the sea god. Another says a saint turned her to stone, face to the sea.

But she speaks too, in a poem over a thousand years old. She was young seven times, its preface says. Then her ebb-tide came.

The poem has her say: what was on flood is all on ebb. So on Beara, her stone still watches the tide, for a flood she does not expect.

stories.title: Irish Halloween customs
stories.hook: Halloween in Ireland was once Snap-Apple Night.
stories.summary: Halloween in Ireland was once Snap-Apple Night. In 1832, painter Daniel Maclise went to a Halloween party in Blarney. It inspired his painting, Snap-Apple Night.
stories.body:
In 1832, painter Daniel Maclise went to a Halloween party in Blarney. It inspired his painting, Snap-Apple Night. In Irish homes, the barmbrack hid a ring, a pea, a stick and a rag.

Whoever got the ring would marry next. Some homes hid one in the colcannon too. Snap apple: an apple swung on a string. Hands behind your back, you tried to bite it.

Two nuts on the hot grate stood for a girl and her sweetheart. If one jumped away, so might the match. A century later, a Blarney schoolboy still called it snap-apple night.

stories.title: Phil Casey & Irish handball
stories.hook: Beaten in Cork, he built his own court.
stories.summary: Beaten in Cork, he built his own court. Phil Casey was born in Mountrath, in what is now County Laois.
stories.body:
Phil Casey was born in Mountrath, in what is now County Laois. He emigrated to Brooklyn, and became America's handball champion.

In 1887, he took on Ireland's champion, Dublin's John Lawlor. The first ten games were in Cork, in a huge court. Lawlor won there.

So Casey built a court in Brooklyn, in under thirty days, a guide later said. It had a back wall, which many Irish courts did not.

There, the guide wrote, Lawlor seemed wholly at sea. Lawlor had won in Cork. But Casey won every game in his own court.

stories.title: Handel's Messiah in Dublin
stories.hook: Handel's Messiah premiered in Dublin, not London.
stories.summary: Handel's Messiah premiered in Dublin, not London. Handel arrived in Dublin in November 1741 to give a season of concerts.
stories.body:
Handel arrived in Dublin in November 1741 to give a season of concerts. On 13 April 1742, Messiah was first performed in a new music hall on Fishamble Street.

Gentlemen were asked to come without swords. Ladies were asked not to wear hoops. About 700 people packed into a hall designed for 600.

It raised about 400 pounds. It went to Mercer's Hospital, an infirmary and jailed debtors. Since 1992, a choir has sung from Messiah on Fishamble Street every 13 April.

stories.title: Sir Hans Sloane
stories.hook: An Irish-born doctor's collection founded the British Museum.
stories.summary: An Irish-born doctor's collection founded the British Museum. Hans Sloane was born in Killyleagh, County Down, in 1660.
stories.body:
Hans Sloane was born in Killyleagh, County Down, in 1660. In 1687, he sailed to Jamaica as the governor's doctor. He collected about 800 plants.

He's credited with bringing milk chocolate to Britain, as a drink. Historians say Jamaicans already drank cocoa with milk. In 1695, he married Elizabeth Rose, heir to Jamaican sugar plantations. Enslaved people worked them, and the profits helped fund his collecting.

He died in 1753, leaving over 71,000 objects to the nation. Parliament paid his heirs £20,000 and founded the British Museum. It opened to the public in 1759, in Montagu House.

stories.title: Ha'penny Bridge
stories.hook: Crossing this bridge used to cost money.
stories.summary: Crossing this bridge used to cost money. Before 1816, there was no bridge at this spot on the Liffey. Just seven run-down ferries, run by William Walsh.
stories.body:
Before 1816, there was no bridge at this spot on the Liffey. Just seven run-down ferries, run by William Walsh. Fix the ferries or build a bridge, he was told. He built one.

The iron was cast in Shropshire, England, in 18 sections. The deal: a halfpenny for every crossing, for 100 years. Turnstiles at both ends.

The toll ended in 1919. The nickname never did. Officially, it's the Liffey Bridge. Dubliners still call it the Ha'penny.

stories.title: Harry Ferguson & the tractor
stories.hook: A County Down man's handshake with Henry Ford.
stories.summary: A County Down man's handshake with Henry Ford. Harry Ferguson grew up on a farm at Growell, near Dromore.
stories.body:
Harry Ferguson grew up on a farm at Growell, near Dromore. Selling tractors, he found that a towed plough could snag and tip them over.

So he patented a linkage that made tractor and plough one unit. He took his tractor to Henry Ford in Dearborn, Michigan, in 1938.

They shook hands: Ford would build, Ferguson would sell. Accounts agree nothing was written down. But Henry Ford's grandson ended the deal. Ferguson said Ford kept his design.

So Ferguson sued for 251 million dollars. In 1952, Ford settled for 9.25 million dollars. A County Down man's handshake had become a court case.

stories.title: Henrietta Street tenements
stories.hook: In 1911, 835 people lived in 15 houses.
stories.summary: In 1911, 835 people lived in 15 houses. In the 1720s, Luke Gardiner laid out Henrietta Street. It was Dublin's earliest Georgian street.
stories.body:
In the 1720s, Luke Gardiner laid out Henrietta Street. It was Dublin's earliest Georgian street. In its first 30 years, it housed three archbishops and a Lord Chancellor.

Later, the King's Inns library rose on the site of an archbishop's house. After union with Britain in 1801, the elite drifted to London. In 1876, number 14 was split into 19 tenement flats.

In 1911, 104 people from 19 families shared number 7. Since 2018, number 14 has been a museum of the lives lived inside it.
