stories.title: The Hill of Slane
stories.hook: Slane's legendary Easter fire broke a king's law.
stories.summary: Slane's legendary Easter fire broke a king's law. Muirchú, an early biographer, wrote it down two centuries after Patrick.
stories.body:
Muirchú, an early biographer, wrote it down two centuries after Patrick. He says King Laoghaire was feasting at Tara that Easter night.

By custom, anyone who lit a fire before the king did would die. But Patrick lit his Easter fire first, and Tara saw it.

The druids warned: put it out tonight, or it will never go out. Yet Muirchú never says the fire was at Slane. Some archaeologists look elsewhere on the Boyne.

Tradition kept the Hill of Slane anyway, and dated the fire to 433. A plaque on the hill says the Easter fire is still lit each year.

stories.title: The Hill of Uisneach
stories.hook: Legend buries Ireland's name under a Westmeath stone.
stories.summary: Legend buries Ireland's name under a Westmeath stone. It is a huge limestone boulder on the Hill of Uisneach.
stories.body:
It is a huge limestone boulder on the Hill of Uisneach. In Irish it is Aill na Míreann, the stone of the divisions.

Those divisions were the provinces. Tradition says all five met at this rock. In the 1180s, Gerald of Wales called a stone here Ireland's navel, its centre.

Keating's history tells how the name came. The Milesians met a queen on Uisneach. Their poet asked her name. She said: I am Ériu, and this island is named after me.

Local tradition says she lies under the stone of divisions. Her name never left the land: Éire, and in English, Ireland.

stories.title: Hook Head Lighthouse
stories.hook: Monks kept this Wexford lighthouse lit for centuries.
stories.summary: Monks kept this Wexford lighthouse lit for centuries. It is about 800 years old. Most accounts say William Marshal built it to guide ships to New Ross.
stories.body:
It is about 800 years old. Most accounts say William Marshal built it to guide ships to New Ross. A stairway of 115 steps runs inside its walls. Monks from Churchtown kept a fire on top.

They tended it until war broke out in 1641. The light went dark, and wrecks followed. It was restored in the 1660s. In 1738, a chart called it a lighthouse of great antiquity.

A popular story says Cromwell vowed to take Waterford by Hook or by Crooke. The phrase is older, from the 1300s. Since 1996 it has lit itself, one of the world's oldest working lighthouses.

stories.title: The origin of 'hooligan'
stories.hook: Nobody can prove who London's first Hooligan was.
stories.summary: Nobody can prove who London's first Hooligan was. Dictionaries trace the name to an Irish surname: Houlihan, or Ó hUallacháin.
stories.body:
Dictionaries trace the name to an Irish surname: Houlihan, or Ó hUallacháin. In the hot summer of 1898, London's papers filled with “Hooligan gangs”.

By September, a reader asked the journal Notes and Queries about the name. A man in court, he wrote, traced it to a comic music-hall song.

Soon the writer Clarence Rook claimed a real man: Patrick Hooligan. Even Rook admitted that legend had been at work on Hooligan's life.

Years later, the Britannica wrote that its true origin had been lost. The word made it into the dictionaries. The first Hooligan never did.

stories.title: Howth Harbour & the 1914 gun-running
stories.hook: In 1914, a yacht landed 900 rifles here.
stories.summary: In 1914, a yacht landed 900 rifles here. Work on Howth Harbour began in 1807, for the mail packets from Holyhead.
stories.body:
Work on Howth Harbour began in 1807, for the mail packets from Holyhead. On 12 August 1821, King George the Fourth landed here, on his 59th birthday.

But silt kept filling the harbour, and steamers grew larger. In 1826, the mail packets moved to Kingstown. On 26 July 1914, Erskine Childers sailed the Asgard into the harbour. Its rifles for the Irish Volunteers were unloaded in broad daylight.

That evening, soldiers fired on a crowd at Bachelors Walk. Three people were killed, and a fourth died later. Since 2012, the Asgard has been on show at Collins Barracks. Howth is now a busy fishing port.

stories.title: Huguenot Dublin
stories.hook: This cathedral once had a French church inside.
stories.summary: This cathedral once had a French church inside. In 1666, Saint Patrick's offered its Lady Chapel to Huguenots, French Protestant refugees. Services ran there until 1816.
stories.body:
In 1666, Saint Patrick's offered its Lady Chapel to Huguenots, French Protestant refugees. Services ran there until 1816. In 1685, Louis the Fourteenth revoked the Edict of Nantes. French Protestants lost all religious and civil liberties.

Soldiers were billeted in Huguenot homes to force conversions. Hundreds of thousands fled France. In Dublin, fellow refugees left their money with former soldier David La Touche. Investing it, he laid the foundations of a bank.

Many Huguenots wove silk and poplin in the Liberties. In 1745, La Touche paid for a new Weavers' Hall there. Their 1693 cemetery survives off St Stephen's Green. You can still see it through railings on Merrion Row.

stories.title: Hurling: Ireland's ancient game
stories.hook: UNESCO says hurling is 2,000 years old.
stories.summary: UNESCO says hurling is 2,000 years old. The GAA says at least 3,000 years in Ireland. Old Brehon Laws set compensation for hurling injuries.
stories.body:
The GAA says at least 3,000 years in Ireland. Old Brehon Laws set compensation for hurling injuries. In one telling, the boy Sétanta killed Culann's guard dog with his sliotar. So he became Cú Chulainn, Culann's Hound.

In 1527, Galway's town council banned “the horlinge of the litill balle”. In 1884, the GAA was founded in Thurles to revive Gaelic games.

Women play camogie, also with a camán and sliotar. Its first official match was in 1904. Kilkenny lead with 36 All-Ireland hurling titles. Then Cork 30, Tipperary 29, and 2026 champions, Limerick, 13.

stories.title: Hy-Brasil, the phantom island
stories.hook: This island west of Ireland never existed.
stories.summary: This island west of Ireland never existed. On the Aran Islands, people said Hy-Brasil could be seen once every seven years.
stories.body:
On the Aran Islands, people said Hy-Brasil could be seen once every seven years. In 1325, a sea chart first drew it as a circle west of Ireland.

Mapmakers copied it for over 500 years. In 1480 and 1481, ships left Bristol to find it. In 1498, a Spanish envoy wrote that Bristol had searched for seven years.

By the 1750s, a London chart called it the Imaginary Isle of O Brazil. Thomas Westropp wrote that, as a boy in 1872, he saw it at sunset. Someone cried that he could see New York. In 1912, he told the Royal Irish Academy it was an illusion.

stories.title: The giant Irish elk
stories.hook: Ireland's giant elk was never an elk.
stories.summary: Ireland's giant elk was never an elk. Its antlers kept turning up in Irish bogs, known as elk horns.
stories.body:
Its antlers kept turning up in Irish bogs, known as elk horns. A Dublin doctor, Thomas Molyneux, set out to end that error.

He measured one head from County Meath: ten foot ten inches across. Elk antlers he saw from Sweden were far smaller. So the name had to go.

Instead, in 1697, he declared them American moose, once common in Ireland. But Europe's elk is America's moose. His fix was the same mistake.

Its DNA points to the fallow deer. Its bones reach Siberia. We still say Irish elk. It was never an elk, and never only Irish.

stories.title: The Irish hare
stories.hook: Ireland's own hare rarely turns white in winter.
stories.summary: Ireland's own hare rarely turns white in winter. It is a mountain hare. Elsewhere, its kin turn white on snowy hills.
stories.body:
It is a mountain hare. Elsewhere, its kin turn white on snowy hills. Its bones in Irish caves show it was here over 28,000 years ago.

Alone here, it grew apart, and a Belfast man noticed. Naturalist William Thompson compared it with Scottish mountain hares.

His 1838 paper said theirs turned white each winter, but Ireland's did not. He saw white ones only in parks, and put it down to age.

Scientists now say the Irish hare can still turn white. It needs the right day length and cold. Mild Irish winters seldom bring that, so it goes grey-brown, not white.

stories.title: Irish words in English
stories.hook: Galore went from Irish into English, and back.
stories.summary: Galore went from Irish into English, and back. P. W. Joyce, a Limerick scholar, traced it to the Irish go leor: plenty.
stories.body:
P. W. Joyce, a Limerick scholar, traced it to the Irish go leor: plenty. Irish people taking up English, he wrote, carried such words with them.

Oxford's great dictionary also traced galore to go leor: enough. In his 1910 book, Joyce said galore now often turned up in English newspapers.

By then the Irish word was at home in English print. But six years earlier, it had come home, in Dinneen's Irish dictionary.

The Kerry priest's entry for go leor gives enough, plenty, in plenty. Then, in quote marks, the English word it had become: galore.

stories.title: Islandbridge Barracks
stories.hook: This Dublin barracks had stabling for 185 horses.
stories.summary: This Dublin barracks had stabling for 185 horses. Islandbridge Barracks went up in 1798, for artillery, beside Sarah Bridge.
stories.body:
Islandbridge Barracks went up in 1798, for artillery, beside Sarah Bridge. By the 1830s, it had room for 23 officers and 547 men.

The Irish Army took it over in December 1922. Its Artillery Corps was formed there in 1923. In 1942 it was renamed for Peadar Clancy, a Volunteer officer from County Clare. He was killed in custody in Dublin Castle in November 1920.

In 1998, the government chose to sell it. Its old buildings by the bridge are now homes. And his name stayed. The new neighbourhood is called Clancy Quay.

stories.title: Jack Kelly & the 1920 Olympic sculls
stories.hook: Henley barred men who worked with their hands.
stories.summary: Henley barred men who worked with their hands. Jack Kelly, son of a Newport, County Mayo man, laid bricks in Philadelphia.
stories.body:
Jack Kelly, son of a Newport, County Mayo man, laid bricks in Philadelphia. By 1920 he was America's rowing champion. He entered Henley's Diamond Sculls race.

Before he could sail, a cable said: not accepted. Letter follows. Henley's minutes gave two reasons: his banned rowing club, and manual labour.

So he said he wanted a crack at whoever won the Diamond Sculls. That was Jack Beresford. They met in the Antwerp Olympic final.

Beresford led by a length. Kelly caught him and won by a second. Too tired to shake hands, the paper said. The bricklayer Henley refused was Olympic champion.

stories.title: James Joyce's Dublin
stories.hook: Joyce's Ulysses takes place on one Dublin day.
stories.summary: Joyce's Ulysses takes place on one Dublin day. It follows Leopold Bloom around Dublin on 16 June 1904.
stories.body:
It follows Leopold Bloom around Dublin on 16 June 1904. Joyce chose the date for his first outing with Nora Barnacle, his future wife.

He claimed that if Dublin was destroyed, it could be rebuilt using his book as a model. Ulysses was published in Paris on 2 February 1922, his 40th birthday.

In 1954, writers set out along its route in horse-drawn cabs. Now every 16 June is Bloomsday, when fans often retrace Bloom's route.

stories.title: Jameson Distillery Bow Street
stories.hook: This distillery made a million gallons a year.
stories.summary: This distillery made a million gallons a year. A distillery stood on Bow Street by 1780. Scottish-born John Jameson managed it, and later owned it.
stories.body:
A distillery stood on Bow Street by 1780. Scottish-born John Jameson managed it, and later owned it. In the 1800s, Dublin's Big Four distillers came to dominate Irish whiskey.

Two of them were Jameson family firms. In June 1875, fire broke out at a whiskey store in the Liberties. Burning whiskey flowed through the streets.

Later accounts say thirteen people died, not from the flames, but from drinking the whiskey. Bow Street closed in 1971. Since 1975, Jameson has been made in Midleton, County Cork.

stories.title: JFK in Wexford
stories.hook: JFK said his Wexford trip took 115 years.
stories.summary: JFK said his Wexford trip took 115 years. In June 1963, he spoke on the quay at New Ross. Banners read "Welcome Home Mr President."
stories.body:
In June 1963, he spoke on the quay at New Ross. Banners read "Welcome Home Mr President." His great-grandfather Patrick had "left here to become a cooper in East Boston," he said.

Then he drove to Dunganstown, Patrick's home farm, for tea with his cousins. He raised a toast "to the Kennedys who went away and to the Kennedys who stayed behind."

In Wexford town, he laid a wreath for Commodore John Barry. He spoke of his pleasure at "being back from whence I came."

Leaving from Shannon, he promised: "I am going to come back." That November, he was killed in Dallas.

stories.title: Commodore John Barry
stories.hook: Commission number one went to a Wexford man.
stories.summary: Commission number one went to a Wexford man. John Barry was born at Tacumshane, County Wexford, in 1745. He went to sea as a boy and settled in Philadelphia.
stories.body:
John Barry was born at Tacumshane, County Wexford, in 1745. He went to sea as a boy and settled in Philadelphia. In 1775 he took command of the brig Lexington. In 1776 she captured the British tender Edward.

In 1797, Washington signed his commission. He stood first on the list of captains. A 1911 book hailed him as the Father of the American Navy. Some give that title to John Paul Jones.

He died near Philadelphia in 1803, aged 58. In 1956, the United States sent him back to Wexford. He stands in bronze on Crescent Quay.

stories.title: John Philip Holland's submarine
stories.hook: The Fenians funded a Clare teacher's submarine.
stories.summary: The Fenians funded a Clare teacher's submarine. John Philip Holland was born in Liscannor in 1841. He taught maths across Ireland.
stories.body:
John Philip Holland was born in Liscannor in 1841. He taught maths across Ireland. In 1873, he sailed for America, already working on a submarine.

Clan na Gael, the Fenians in America, paid for his early boats. They hoped to use them against Britain's navy. A newspaper nicknamed one the Fenian Ram. Then he fell out with the Clan over money and ownership.

In 1900, the US Navy bought his latest boat. As USS Holland, it was the Navy's first commissioned submarine. A year later, the Royal Navy launched its first submarine. It was a Holland design too.

stories.title: John Tyndall & greenhouse gases
stories.hook: A Carlow man measured which gases trap heat.
stories.summary: A Carlow man measured which gases trap heat. John Tyndall was born in Leighlinbridge, Co Carlow.
stories.body:
John Tyndall was born in Leighlinbridge, Co Carlow. From 1859, in London, he passed heat through a tube of gas.

Water vapour and carbon dioxide soaked it up. Any change in them, he wrote, must change the climate. In America, Eunice Foote had reported a similar effect in 1856. His tests went much further.

In a lit tube, he made a cloud glow sky blue. He put it down to dust and mist, but air molecules make the sky blue. A keen climber, he was the first to climb the Weisshorn in 1861. Today, a British climate centre bears his name. So does Cork's Tyndall National Institute.

stories.title: Kilkenny Castle
stories.hook: Kilkenny Castle once sold for just £50.
stories.summary: Kilkenny Castle once sold for just £50. An 1832 journal dates Strongbow's first castle here to 1172. William Marshal later rebuilt it in stone.
stories.body:
An 1832 journal dates Strongbow's first castle here to 1172. William Marshal later rebuilt it in stone. In about 1391, James Butler, 3rd Earl of Ormond, bought it. It was the Butler seat for nearly 600 years.

In 1650, Cromwell's cannon breached Kilkenny's walls. The town and castle were handed over on 28 March. It was remodelled in the 1800s. A grand Picture Gallery was added for the family's paintings.

In 1967, Lord Ormonde sold the empty castle for £50. He reportedly said Ireland already had too many ruins. On 11 August 1967, it was handed over to the people of Kilkenny.

stories.title: The 1798 landing at Killala
stories.hook: A French general promised freedom within a month.
stories.summary: A French general promised freedom within a month. In August 1798, over 1,000 French troops landed at Kilcummin, County Mayo.
stories.body:
In August 1798, over 1,000 French troops landed at Kilcummin, County Mayo. General Humbert moved into the Bishop of Killala's house.

Bishop Stock spoke French and wrote down his words. Ireland would be free within a month, Humbert said.

Days later, Humbert's French and Irish force routed the army at Castlebar. The army's flight became known as the Races of Castlebar.

But the main French fleet came too late. Humbert surrendered at Ballinamuck, Longford. His soldiers became prisoners of war. Many Irish with him were killed. He promised a month. A month and a day after he landed, the army retook Killala.

stories.title: Killarney's native red deer
stories.hook: Killarney once chased stags into its lake.
stories.summary: Killarney once chased stags into its lake. Hounds drove a stag off the mountain, and visitors' boats followed.
stories.body:
Hounds drove a stag off the mountain, and visitors' boats followed. Mr and Mrs Hall printed one such hunt. It ended when the monarch of Torc fell.

Torc mountain alone held many hundreds of deer, the account said. But shooting went on. By the 1960s, one estimate put them under a hundred.

Kerry volunteers helped bring them back. In 2012, a DNA study traced their origin.

Stone Age farmers brought them from Britain, about 5,000 years ago. Every other Irish herd, the park says, is later stock. The stag in that lake came from Ireland's oldest herd. Its kind still roam Torc.

stories.title: Killiney Hill Obelisk
stories.hook: Killiney's obelisk was built after a hard year.
stories.summary: Killiney's obelisk was built after a hard year. The Great Frost gripped Ireland in early 1740. It destroyed the potatoes, then drought ruined the grain.
stories.body:
The Great Frost gripped Ireland in early 1740. It destroyed the potatoes, then drought ruined the grain. Famine killed hundreds of thousands. Folk memory calls the worst year Bliain an Áir, the year of slaughter.

Then, on Killiney Hill in south Dublin, landowner John Mapas began to build. On the summit, a tall stone cone rose above the bay.

Tradition says he built it to give the hungry paid work. Nearly a century on, a Dublin journal said the obelisk was just for the view. But its marble plaque, dated June 1742, gives the reason. Last year being hard with the poor.

stories.title: Royal Hospital Kilmainham ceiling
stories.hook: This Dublin ceiling is now a papier-mâché copy.
stories.summary: This Dublin ceiling is now a papier-mâché copy. These photos show the original, in the Royal Hospital Kilmainham chapel. It was moulded in plaster in the 1680s.
stories.body:
These photos show the original, in the Royal Hospital Kilmainham chapel. It was moulded in plaster in the 1680s. In 1834, a Dublin paper praised its stucco fruit, flowers and cherubim.

A 1906 account says each flower was moulded on its own blackthorn or oak twig. Some could swing like a pendulum. Its timber frame sagged under the weight. By 1843 it was unsafe, and damp rotted it.

A firm called Jacksons remade it in papier-mâché and fibrous plaster. It weighed about a tenth as much. The oak carving was once said to be by Grinling Gibbons. Historians now credit a Frenchman, James Tabary.

stories.title: Kilmainham Gaol
stories.hook: This jail held rebels for over a century.
stories.summary: This jail held rebels for over a century. It was built in 1796 as the new county gaol.
stories.body:
It was built in 1796 as the new county gaol. Rebels from 1798, 1803 and 1848 were held here. So was Charles Stewart Parnell.

Children were locked up too, for petty theft. The youngest was said to be three. After the Easter Rising, 14 of its leaders were executed in the prison yard.

It closed as a prison in 1924, and fell into ruin. In 1960, volunteers began restoring it. It opened to the public in 1966.

stories.title: The Battle of Kinsale (1601)
stories.hook: Even his enemies praised his march to Kinsale.
stories.summary: Even his enemies praised his march to Kinsale. In 1601, Spanish troops landed at Kinsale, County Cork, and were besieged.
stories.body:
In 1601, Spanish troops landed at Kinsale, County Cork, and were besieged. So Red Hugh O'Donnell of Donegal marched south to free them.

In Tipperary, Carew's army blocked his road, leaving only a boggy mountain. Then a great frost froze it, and he crossed by night.

Carew's chronicle called it the greatest march with baggage ever heard of. With Hugh O'Neill, they attacked on Christmas Eve, by English reckoning.

One historian says the battle was over within two hours. Beaten, Red Hugh sailed to Spain for help and died there within a year. The book that praised his march also mapped his defeat.

stories.title: Kylemore Abbey
stories.hook: Kylemore Abbey was never built as an abbey.
stories.summary: Kylemore Abbey was never built as an abbey. Mitchell Henry and his wife Margaret honeymooned in Connemara, Co Galway. Rich from an inheritance, he quit surgery and bought Kylemore.
stories.body:
Mitchell Henry and his wife Margaret honeymooned in Connemara, Co Galway. Rich from an inheritance, he quit surgery and bought Kylemore. In 1867, Margaret laid the castle's foundation stone.

In 1874, Margaret fell ill on a family trip to Egypt. She died, leaving nine children. In her memory, her husband built a church like a tiny cathedral. It was finished in 1881.

Irish Benedictine nuns had run an abbey in Ypres, Belgium, since 1682. The First World War drove them out and ruined their abbey. In 1920, they bought the castle and renamed it Kylemore Abbey. Nuns still live there today.

stories.title: Sheridan Le Fanu's Carmilla
stories.hook: Before Dracula, a Dubliner wrote a female vampire.
stories.summary: Before Dracula, a Dubliner wrote a female vampire. Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu was born in Dublin in 1814. He is best remembered for his ghost stories.
stories.body:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu was born in Dublin in 1814. He is best remembered for his ghost stories. His wife died in 1858. He was said to be reclusive, and Dublin nicknamed him the Invisible Prince.

In 1871, a magazine called The Dark Blue began printing Carmilla. In a lonely castle in Styria, a family takes in a young stranger. She is a vampire.

Bram Stoker wrote theatre reviews for the Dublin Evening Mail, a paper Le Fanu had part-owned. Le Fanu died at home on Merrion Square in 1873. He never saw Dracula. Dracula appeared in 1897. Stoker's early notes had set it in Styria, Carmilla's country.

stories.title: Leinster House
stories.hook: The White House borrowed from a Dublin mansion.
stories.summary: The White House borrowed from a Dublin mansion. Leinster House was built from 1745, for James FitzGerald, Earl of Kildare.
stories.body:
Leinster House was built from 1745, for James FitzGerald, Earl of Kildare. It stood on the city's unfashionable south side. The Earl predicted others would follow.

In 1766, he became the first Duke of Leinster, and the house took that name. Irish architect James Hoban based parts of the White House's upper floors on it.

In 1815, the third Duke sold it to the Royal Dublin Society. Since 1922, it has been the home of Ireland's parliament.

stories.title: Lord Kelvin of Belfast
stories.hook: Cold is measured in a Belfast man's name.
stories.summary: Cold is measured in a Belfast man's name. William Thomson was born in Belfast in 1824. His father taught maths at the Academical Institution.
stories.body:
William Thomson was born in Belfast in 1824. His father taught maths at the Academical Institution. When William was eight, his father became a Glasgow professor. William started university there at ten.

There, in 1848, he proposed an absolute temperature scale. It depended on no single substance. His footnote reasoned that infinite cold lies about 273 degrees below zero.

Back then, he signed himself William Thomson. The Atlantic cable later made him Sir William. Made a lord, he took his title from the River Kelvin, below his university. From then on, he signed himself Kelvin. Cold is still measured in that name.

stories.title: St. Patrick's Purgatory, Lough Derg
stories.hook: Medieval Europe thought a Donegal cave reached purgatory.
stories.summary: Medieval Europe thought a Donegal cave reached purgatory. The tale said Christ showed it to Patrick, on an island in Lough Derg.
stories.body:
The tale said Christ showed it to Patrick, on an island in Lough Derg. Stay inside a day and a night, it promised, and be purged of sin.

So the monks locked each pilgrim in until morning. The knight Owein's tale of what he saw inside crossed Europe.

Even printed maps abroad marked it by name. But the Annals of Ulster say a Pope's authority had the cave destroyed in 1497.

The cave was rebuilt until a church replaced it. And pilgrims kept coming. They still come for three days, barefoot and fasting. The cave is gone. But they still keep the night awake, in the church.

stories.title: The legend of Lough Neagh
stories.hook: Lough Neagh, they say, began with one handful.
stories.summary: Lough Neagh, they say, began with one handful. A Belfast magazine printed the tale in 1825.
stories.body:
A Belfast magazine printed the tale in 1825. Finn McCool, it said, flung a handful of earth into the sea.

Where the handful fell, it formed the Isle of Man. The hollow it left became Lough Neagh.

Later tellings aimed the throw at a giant on the Scottish shore. It fell short. People said the island was the lough's exact size and shape.

So measure them: the lough is the largest lake in Ireland and Britain. It covers about 150 square miles. The Isle of Man covers about 220. On the map, the handful is bigger than the hole it left.

stories.title: Louis Brennan's gyroscopic monorail
stories.hook: This car could stand still on one rail.
stories.summary: This car could stand still on one rail. Louis Brennan left Castlebar for Melbourne at nine.
stories.body:
Louis Brennan left Castlebar for Melbourne at nine. There he invented a torpedo steered by wires.

Britain's War Office bought it, for a reported 110,000 pounds. With that fortune, he built a model car in his Gillingham garden.

Spinning gyroscopes kept it upright, even on a wire. A full-size car followed, carrying dozens of passengers.

Winston Churchill is said to have taken a ride on it in London in 1910. But investors feared the gyroscopes might fail, and left.

Brennan died in Montreux in 1932, hit by a car. His monorail could keep its balance. The world never trusted one rail.

stories.title: The Lusitania & Kinsale
stories.hook: Kinsale's old courthouse heard the Lusitania's captain.
stories.summary: Kinsale's old courthouse heard the Lusitania's captain. On 7 May 1915, a U-boat torpedoed the liner off the Old Head of Kinsale.
stories.body:
On 7 May 1915, a U-boat torpedoed the liner off the Old Head of Kinsale. She sank in about 18 minutes. About 1,200 people died.

That evening the patrol boat Heron brought five of the dead into Kinsale. Coroner John Horgan opened an inquest at the courthouse on 8 May.

On 10 May, Captain William Turner gave evidence. He described one torpedo, then a second explosion. A jury of 14 shopkeepers and fishermen returned a verdict of wilful murder. Half an hour later, an order came to stop Turner testifying. Horgan wrote that it came too late.

stories.title: Lynch's Window in Galway
stories.hook: This window claims Galway's mayor hanged his son.
stories.summary: This window claims Galway's mayor hanged his son. Its stones came from a Lynch family house.
stories.body:
Its stones came from a Lynch family house. Legend links it to James Lynch FitzStephen, mayor in 1493.

His son Walter, the story goes, killed a Spanish guest. Later tellings say no one would carry out the sentence.

So, the tale says, the mayor hanged Walter from his own window. But historians find no record of it from the time.

Yet when the house came down, a committee kept the stones. In 1854, they were rebuilt into a Market Street wall.

A panel claims the mayor executed his guilty son on this spot. So Galway kept the window, whether or not the hanging happened.

stories.title: Dublin's Mansion House
stories.hook: This house's seller was owed sugar every Christmas.
stories.summary: This house's seller was owed sugar every Christmas. Joshua Dawson laid out Dawson Street in 1707. This was meant to be his townhouse.
stories.body:
Joshua Dawson laid out Dawson Street in 1707. This was meant to be his townhouse. In 1715, he sold it to Dublin Corporation as the Lord Mayor's home. The deal also promised him a sugar loaf every Christmas.

In 1821, the Round Room was built in just 6 weeks, for a visit by King George the Fourth. On 21 January 1919, the First Dáil met in that room.

There, Ireland's Declaration of Independence was read in Irish, English and French. In 2015, a Dawson descendant finally collected a sugar loaf. It is still the Lord Mayor's official residence.

stories.title: Marconi at Dún Laoghaire
stories.hook: Marconi reported Dún Laoghaire's regatta from the sea.
stories.summary: Marconi reported Dún Laoghaire's regatta from the sea. In July 1898, the town was still Kingstown. The Dublin Daily Express wanted the races as they happened.
stories.body:
In July 1898, the town was still Kingstown. The Dublin Daily Express wanted the races as they happened. A hired steamer, the Flying Huntress, followed the yachts out to sea. Its transmitter tapped each race ashore in Morse.

A 110-foot mast at Kingstown caught signals from up to 25 miles out. Each message was phoned to Dublin. Readers followed races with the yachts out of sight of land. One 1899 account counts over 700 messages.

Oxford's Marconi archive calls it the first wireless report of a sporting event. Marconi was half Irish. His mother, Annie, came from Enniscorthy, Co Wexford.

stories.title: Constance Markievicz (1918)
stories.hook: One woman won in 1918: an Irish prisoner.
stories.summary: One woman won in 1918: an Irish prisoner. Constance Gore-Booth grew up at Lissadell House, County Sligo. She married a Polish artist, becoming known as Countess Markievicz.
stories.body:
Constance Gore-Booth grew up at Lissadell House, County Sligo. She married a Polish artist, becoming known as Countess Markievicz. In 1916, she fought in the Rising at St Stephen's Green. Sentenced to death, she was spared because she was a woman.

In December 1918, she won Dublin St Patrick's while held in Holloway. She was the first woman elected to Westminster. Like the other Sinn Féin MPs, she never took her seat.

Freed in 1919, she became Minister for Labour in the Dáil. She was one of Europe's first women government ministers. No other woman sat in an Irish cabinet until 1979.

stories.title: Marsh's Library
stories.hook: Readers next door could be locked in cages.
stories.summary: Readers next door could be locked in cages. Marsh's Library opened in 1707, as Ireland's first public library.
stories.body:
Marsh's Library opened in 1707, as Ireland's first public library. Archbishop Narcissus Marsh founded it, beside Saint Patrick's Cathedral.

By the mid-1760s, over 1,000 books were missing. So readers were watched at a table, or locked in cages.

In 1866, Trinity College student Bram Stoker came here to read. On 30 April 1916, a British machine gun nearby sprayed it with bullets. It is one of the last eighteenth-century buildings in Ireland still used for its original purpose.

stories.title: Dublin's Martello towers
stories.hook: Dublin's towers waited for Napoleon. He never came.
stories.summary: Dublin's towers waited for Napoleon. He never came. In 1804, Britain feared Napoleon would invade Ireland. Towers and gun batteries went up along Dublin's coast.
stories.body:
In 1804, Britain feared Napoleon would invade Ireland. Towers and gun batteries went up along Dublin's coast. They stood at 28 sites, from Bray to Balbriggan. Most were built within sight of each other.

The name comes from a tower at Mortella, in Corsica. The British got the name wrong. Their walls were stronger on the side facing the sea. The only door was high up, reached by a removable ladder.

In 1904, James Joyce stayed briefly in the Sandycove tower. Ulysses opens there. Today, most of the sites survive. Howth's tower now houses a vintage radio museum.

stories.title: Martin Sheridan, Mayo's Olympian
stories.hook: Mayo's Sheridan beat Greece at its own discus.
stories.summary: Mayo's Sheridan beat Greece at its own discus. Martin Sheridan left Bohola for New York. At St Louis, he won Olympic discus gold.
stories.body:
Martin Sheridan left Bohola for New York. At St Louis, he won Olympic discus gold. In London in 1908, now a New York policeman, he won again.

But London also held a Greek-style discus, thrown from a sloping pedestal. Greece had brought that style to its Athens Games two years earlier.

He stepped onto the pedestal, and won that too. The official report noted no Greek finished in the first four.

Ten years later, in 1918, Sheridan died of pneumonia in New York, aged 36. The Greek discus never returned to the Games. Its last Olympic champion was a Mayo man.

stories.title: Queen Medb & the cattle raid
stories.hook: A queen went to war over pillow talk.
stories.summary: A queen went to war over pillow talk. At Cruachan, Roscommon, the tale says, Medb and Ailill argued in bed. Who was richer?
stories.body:
At Cruachan, Roscommon, the tale says, Medb and Ailill argued in bed. Who was richer? They counted everything. All equal, except Ailill's bull, the White-horned.

Born in Medb's herd, he would not be owned by a woman. His match was in Cooley, County Louth. “Brown he is, and dark as night.”

The owner refused to lend him. Medb marched on Ulster. Many died. At Cruachan, the bulls fought into the night.

The Brown Bull won, scattering his rival across Ireland. The tale names Athlone for the loin. His heart broke. Two bulls dead, the count equal again, all from pillow talk.

stories.title: Mellifont Abbey
stories.hook: Mellifont began as a few grains of seed.
stories.summary: Mellifont began as a few grains of seed. In 1142, Malachy of Armagh founded Mellifont in County Louth. It was Ireland's first Cistercian abbey.
stories.body:
In 1142, Malachy of Armagh founded Mellifont in County Louth. It was Ireland's first Cistercian abbey. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux in France, sent monks to start it.

Those monks, he wrote, were only a few grains of seed. But the French monks soon went home. Bernard wrote that he wished they had stayed.

Perhaps, he told Malachy, the Irish brothers were partly the reason. So he sent their Irish abbot back to them, with one monk, Robert, to help build. Today, part of Mellifont's eight-sided wash house still stands. That seed, Bernard wrote, grew into five daughter houses.

stories.title: Merrion Square
stories.hook: A cathedral was once planned for this park.
stories.summary: A cathedral was once planned for this park. Merrion Square was laid out in 1762, for the Fitzwilliam estate. Building went on for 30 years.
stories.body:
Merrion Square was laid out in 1762, for the Fitzwilliam estate. Building went on for 30 years. Georgian red-brick houses line three sides. Doorcases and ironwork gave the houses their own character.

Daniel O'Connell lived at number 58. The poet Yeats lived at number 82 from 1922 to 1928. In 1930, the Catholic Church bought the park as a site for a cathedral. It was never built.

On 2 February 1972, protests followed Bloody Sunday in Derry. The British Embassy at number 39 was burned. In April 1974, the archbishop handed the park over. Today, it is a public park.

stories.title: Merrow sea legends
stories.hook: A Kerry tale: a stolen cap, a sea-bride.
stories.summary: A Kerry tale: a stolen cap, a sea-bride. Yeats wrote that the merrow, Ireland's sea-woman, has a red cap. Without it, she cannot dive.
stories.body:
Yeats wrote that the merrow, Ireland's sea-woman, has a red cap. Without it, she cannot dive. Croker noted a Kerry belief: the O'Flahertys and O'Sullivans had merrow blood.

In Croker's tale, a merrow combs her sea-green hair by Smerwick Harbour. Dick Fitzgerald seizes her little enchanted cap from the strand.

Without the cap, she cannot go home. They marry and have three children. One day, with Dick away, she pulls down a fishing net. Behind it, in a hole in the wall, is her cap. At the strand, she puts on the cap and plunges in. Dick never sees her again.

stories.hook: Molly Malone may never have existed.
stories.summary: Molly Malone may never have existed. The earliest known printing of the song is from 1876, in Boston.
stories.body:
The earliest known printing of the song is from 1876, in Boston. A London edition in 1884 credits James Yorkston of Edinburgh.

There is no evidence she was a real woman. Still, in 1988, Dublin declared 13 June Molly Malone Day.

That year, Jeanne Rynhart's statue went up on Grafton Street. In 2014, she moved to Suffolk Street. Locals call her the Tart with the Cart.

stories.title: The Mourne Wall
stories.hook: A Mourne wall climbs mountains to stop sheep.
stories.summary: A Mourne wall climbs mountains to stop sheep. The reason was Belfast's water. Its linen mills and shipyards needed more.
stories.body:
The reason was Belfast's water. Its linen mills and shipyards needed more. So the Water Commissioners bought 9,000 Mourne acres, for the rain.

But grazing cattle and sheep could foul that water, and nothing filtered it. So, in 1904, stonemen began walling the whole catchment.

They split granite on the spot and made their own chisels. The wall crossed 15 summits, Slieve Donard among them, for about 22 miles.

Eighteen years on, in 1922, it was done. Then the Silent Valley reservoir was built inside it. Built to stop sheep, it still encircles the rain much of Belfast drinks.

stories.title: Muckross House
stories.hook: This Kerry house was a California wedding present.
stories.summary: This Kerry house was a California wedding present. Muckross House, near Killarney, was finished in 1843 for the Herbert family.
stories.body:
Muckross House, near Killarney, was finished in 1843 for the Herbert family. In August 1861, Queen Victoria stayed two nights. The house was lavishly redone for her.

The Herberts' son Henry lost the estate to debt by 1899. Tradition blames the cost of that royal visit. In 1911, it was bought by William Bourn of Filoli, California. It was a wedding gift for his daughter Maud.

Maud died in 1929. In 1932, her parents and husband gave the whole estate to the nation. That wedding present became Ireland's first national park.

stories.title: Muiredach's High Cross
stories.hook: Two stone cats frame a name in Louth.
stories.summary: Two stone cats frame a name in Louth. They sit at the foot of a high cross at Monasterboice. It's usually dated to the early 900s.
stories.body:
They sit at the foot of a high cross at Monasterboice. It's usually dated to the early 900s. Between them, Irish letters ask a prayer for Muiredach, who had the cross made. He was probably the abbot here.

Above them, panels climb the shaft to the Crucifixion in the ring. On the east face, David fights Goliath, and Moses strikes water from a rock.

Scholars often call them sermons in stone, a Bible for those who couldn't read. Others think they spoke mainly to monks. About 1,100 years on, one cat still licks her kitten beside his name.

stories.title: National Gallery of Ireland
stories.hook: Dublin Jesuits dined beneath a lost Caravaggio.
stories.summary: Dublin Jesuits dined beneath a lost Caravaggio. The National Gallery grew out of Dublin's 1853 Great Industrial Exhibition. It opened in 1864, with just 112 paintings.
stories.body:
The National Gallery grew out of Dublin's 1853 Great Industrial Exhibition. It opened in 1864, with just 112 paintings. In 1944, George Bernard Shaw said he owed it much of the only real education he got as a boy.

When he died in 1950, he left the gallery a third of his royalties. In 1956, his play Pygmalion became the musical My Fair Lady. The royalties soared.

In 1990, a gallery conservator examined the Jesuits' dark painting. It was Caravaggio's lost Taking of Christ. The Jesuits lent it to the gallery indefinitely. Today, the collection is free to visit.

stories.title: Navan Fort (Emain Macha)
stories.hook: One Armagh oak dated a legendary royal mound.
stories.summary: One Armagh oak dated a legendary royal mound. The mound is at Navan Fort, Emain Macha of the tales, Ulster's royal seat.
stories.body:
The mound is at Navan Fort, Emain Macha of the tales, Ulster's royal seat. Old annals say Queen Macha built it as Ulster's chief city.

One historian rejected that story as fable. In the 1960s, Dudley Waterman dug into the mound. Under it lay a 40-metre round timber building, around one great oak post.

Its builders filled it with limestone, burned it, and buried it in turf. Nobody knows why. But deep in damp clay, the oak's base survived.

At Queen's in Belfast, its rings were read: felled in 95 BC. Ulster's kings may stay legend. Their mound has a date, from one oak.

stories.title: Nelson's Pillar
stories.hook: Before the Spire, there was Nelson.
stories.summary: Before the Spire, there was Nelson. In 1809, a column with Admiral Nelson on top opened on Sackville Street. Now O'Connell Street.
stories.body:
In 1809, a column with Admiral Nelson on top opened on Sackville Street. Now O'Connell Street. 168 steps inside. For a small fee, you could climb to the top.

In 1916, the GPO beside it burned. Nelson stayed up. Then, at 1:32 a.m. on 8 March 1966, a bomb blew the top off. No one was hurt.

Six days later, the Army blew up what was left. Art students stole Nelson's head. It's now in the Dublin City Library and Archive on Pearse Street. In 2003, the Spire went up on the same spot. 120 metres.

stories.title: Newgrange
stories.hook: This Meath tomb is older than the pyramids.
stories.summary: This Meath tomb is older than the pyramids. Newgrange was built around 3200 BC. The Great Pyramid of Giza came centuries later.
stories.body:
Newgrange was built around 3200 BC. The Great Pyramid of Giza came centuries later. In 1699, workmen digging for stone found the entrance. The stone in front is carved with spirals.

Above the door is a small opening, the roof box. Locals said the tomb filled with sunlight at midwinter. In 1967, archaeologist Michael O'Kelly waited inside on solstice morning. Sunlight streamed through the roof box and lit the chamber.

The light lasts about 17 minutes. Each year, thousands apply to be inside. Stone Age people aimed this tomb at the midwinter sunrise. Over 5,000 years later, it still works.

stories.title: O'Connell Bridge
stories.hook: This bridge is wider than it is long.
stories.summary: This bridge is wider than it is long. It opened in 1794 as Carlisle Bridge, designed by James Gandon.
stories.body:
It opened in 1794 as Carlisle Bridge, designed by James Gandon. It was narrow and humped. By the mid 1800s, traffic had shaken it to its foundations.

In 1877, engineer Bindon Blood Stoney began a new bridge, almost 3 times as wide. Traffic kept crossing the old bridge while new sections went up on each side.

Work finished in 1880. It was renamed for Daniel O'Connell. Today it is about 50 metres wide, and only about 45 metres long.

stories.title: O'Connell's monster meeting at Tara
stories.hook: Nobody agrees how many people came to Tara.
stories.summary: Nobody agrees how many people came to Tara. On 15 August 1843, Daniel O'Connell held a monster meeting at Tara, Co Meath. He wanted the Act of Union repealed.
stories.body:
On 15 August 1843, Daniel O'Connell held a monster meeting at Tara, Co Meath. He wanted the Act of Union repealed. The Nation newspaper said 750,000. Others claimed over a million.

A historian suggests such figures could be cut by up to 75 per cent. One supporter said people cared little for speeches they could read next day.

O'Connell called a meeting at Clontarf, Dublin, for 8 October. The government banned it the night before. He called it off and sent messengers to turn the crowds back. Within a week, he was charged with conspiracy.

stories.title: Ogham stones
stories.hook: The oldest written Irish is notches on stone.
stories.summary: The oldest written Irish is notches on stone. Kerry has about a third of all ogham stones. Most date from about the 4th to the 7th century.
stories.body:
Kerry has about a third of all ogham stones. Most date from about the 4th to the 7th century. Each letter is a set of notches or strokes cut along the stone's edge. You read it from the bottom up.

The tallest, at Ballycrovane in Cork, stands about 4.7 metres. At Dunloe, near Killarney, the strokes come in bundles of one to five. Most stones give a name and a father.

Seven Dunloe stones were found in 1838, reused to roof an underground passage. Their word for son, MAQI, lives on as Mac in Irish surnames.

stories.title: Oisín & Tír na nÓg
stories.hook: One golden girth cost Oisín 300 years.
stories.summary: One golden girth cost Oisín 300 years. The old tale ends in Glenasmole, County Dublin.
stories.body:
The old tale ends in Glenasmole, County Dublin. Niamh, on a white horse, carried Oisín over the sea to Tír na nÓg.

It felt like three years, one telling says. In Ireland, 300 went by. Niamh let him ride home. One foot on the ground, she warned, and you never come back.

In Glenasmole, men strained at a great stone. From the saddle, he flung it. The golden girth snapped. His two feet hit the ground.

The horse fled, and every one of those years fell on him. Blind, he told it all to Patrick. That broken girth is why the story survives.

stories.title: Oscar Wilde in Dublin
stories.hook: Dublin waited 97 years for a Wilde statue.
stories.summary: Dublin waited 97 years for a Wilde statue. Oscar Wilde was born at 21 Westland Row in 1854.
stories.body:
Oscar Wilde was born at 21 Westland Row in 1854. In 1855, the family moved to Number 1 Merrion Square.

Guests at their salon included Sheridan Le Fanu and William Rowan Hamilton. At Trinity College, he won the Berkeley Gold Medal in Greek. It was Trinity's top prize in Greek.

He died in Paris in 1900. In 1997, a statue was unveiled near his childhood home. It is made of coloured stones from three continents. It wears a porcelain Trinity tie.

stories.title: Dr. Pat O'Callaghan
stories.hook: Cork doctor won independent Ireland's first Olympic gold.
stories.summary: Cork doctor won independent Ireland's first Olympic gold. Pat O'Callaghan, from near Kanturk, was a doctor at 20. He learned the hammer in Dublin.
stories.body:
Pat O'Callaghan, from near Kanturk, was a doctor at 20. He learned the hammer in Dublin. Until 1928, Americans won every Olympic hammer title, most of them Irish-born.

He won by ten centimetres on 30 July 1928. Accounts say he used the Swedish leader's hammer. The New York Times front page next day: Irishman Takes Hammer Throw.

Photos show the tricolour on the centre mast. Irish accounts call it an Olympic first. In Los Angeles in 1932, his spikes kept catching on the cinder circle. Team Ireland says a teammate, fresh from his own gold, helped file them. Pat won again with his last throw.

stories.title: Phoenix Park
stories.hook: This park is twice Central Park's size.
stories.summary: This park is twice Central Park's size. Phoenix Park covers 707 hectares, inside an 11-kilometre wall.
stories.body:
Phoenix Park covers 707 hectares, inside an 11-kilometre wall. In 1662, the Duke of Ormond began turning it into a royal hunting park.

Around 400 fallow deer still roam here, descended from deer introduced in the 1660s. In 1745, the Earl of Chesterfield opened it to the public.

The Wellington Monument is 62 metres tall, the largest obelisk in Europe. In 1979, over a million people gathered here for Pope John Paul the Second's Mass.

stories.title: The Pigeon House
stories.hook: The Pigeon House was named after a man.
stories.summary: The Pigeon House was named after a man. In 1761, John Pidgeon became caretaker of a South Wall storehouse.
stories.body:
In 1761, John Pidgeon became caretaker of a South Wall storehouse. His family served refreshments to travellers. The storehouse became known as the Pigeon House.

In 1793, work began on a grand hotel here, facing its own harbour. After the 1798 rebellion, soldiers took it over. It became Pigeon House Fort, guarded by drawbridges and guns.

In 1897, the fort was sold to Dublin Corporation. A power station here first made electricity in July 1903. In the 1970s, the Poolbeg chimneys rose beside it, over 200 metres tall. Locals still call the site the Pigeon House.

stories.title: The Plassy wreck, Inis Oírr
stories.hook: Every man aboard this Aran Islands wreck survived.
stories.summary: Every man aboard this Aran Islands wreck survived. Early on 8 March 1960, the cargo ship Plassy hit Finnis Rock off Inis Oírr.
stories.body:
Early on 8 March 1960, the cargo ship Plassy hit Finnis Rock off Inis Oírr. A gale was blowing, and the 11 men on board were trapped.

Word reached the village, and about 60 islanders turned out to help. They had a breeches buoy: a lifebuoy with canvas shorts, on a rope. It had never been used there.

A rocket carried a line out to the ship. One by one, all 11 were hauled ashore. Later storms threw the ship up onto the shore, where it still sits. It's the wreck in the opening titles of Father Ted.

stories.title: Poolbeg Lighthouse & Great South Wall
stories.hook: Dublin built a wall into the sea.
stories.summary: Dublin built a wall into the sea. Sand and silt kept building up where the Liffey met the bay. Ships waited for high tide to cross.
stories.body:
Sand and silt kept building up where the Liffey met the bay. Ships waited for high tide to cross. In 1715, work began on a barrier of oak piles. It ran from Ringsend out into the bay.

Storms broke the timber. In 1761, a stone wall was begun at the far end, working back to shore. The lighthouse was first lit on 29 September 1767. Candles gave way to oil in 1786.

The granite wall was finished in 1795. It is still one of Europe's longest sea walls. Low tide here on 8 April 1837 became zero for Irish map heights. The light still guides ships today.

stories.title: Powerscourt Waterfall
stories.hook: A king never reached this waterfall's bridge.
stories.summary: A king never reached this waterfall's bridge. The king was George IV, due at Powerscourt in 1821, on his last day in Ireland.
stories.body:
The king was George IV, due at Powerscourt in 1821, on his last day in Ireland. His host, Lord Powerscourt, wanted the fall in full flood. The family's history says a dam was built above it.

The king would stand on the bridge as a mine blew the dam. But the king never got there. He stayed at a banquet in the house, and time ran out.

Afterwards the mine was fired anyway. The water came down and carried the bridge away. The king's bridge was gone. In 1903, his host's grandson wrote: a fearful catastrophe was averted.

stories.title: Printing the 1916 Proclamation
stories.hook: Dublin, 1916: the Proclamation ran short of e's.
stories.summary: Dublin, 1916: the Proclamation ran short of e's. Its type was set in Liberty Hall on Easter Sunday, 23 April.
stories.body:
Its type was set in Liberty Hall on Easter Sunday, 23 April. Christopher Brady ran the old Wharfedale press. Michael Molloy and Liam O'Brien set the type.

Their type, mostly borrowed, would not cover the whole text. So they printed the top half first. Then they reset the type and printed the bottom half. Brady said they ran off 2,500 copies.

Short of e's, they used smaller ones from another font. Brady even turned an F into an E with sealing wax. British soldiers later found the bottom half still on the press. They reportedly printed “half proclamations” as souvenirs.

stories.title: The púca
stories.hook: Don't pick blackberries after Halloween. Here's why.
stories.summary: Don't pick blackberries after Halloween. Here's why. In the 1930s, a Kildare granny warned her granddaughter. Never eat them after Halloween: the púca soils them.
stories.body:
In the 1930s, a Kildare granny warned her granddaughter. Never eat them after Halloween: the púca soils them. The púca was Irish folklore's great shape-shifter. At Samhain it was said to roam, often as a dark horse.

In 1888, WB Yeats recorded it too. After November Eve, he wrote, the púca has spoiled the blackberries. It is on the map too. Poulaphouca, Co Wicklow, comes from Poll an Phúca: the púca's hole or pool.

A 1987 placenames study counted 19 places called Poll an Phúca across Ireland. So why the rule? The National Museum says it was meant to keep children off bad berries.

stories.title: The puffins of Skellig Michael
stories.hook: Each August, Skellig's puffins vanish from the rock.
stories.summary: Each August, Skellig's puffins vanish from the rock. Off Kerry, the Skellig lighthouse keepers logged birds.
stories.body:
Off Kerry, the Skellig lighthouse keepers logged birds. Their entry for 1888 reads, "Puffins first landed on rock."

Logs like theirs showed a punctual bird: in by late March, gone by mid-August. But once it flew off, no keeper could see where it went.

So in 2010, University College Cork scientists put trackers on Skellig puffins. Most of the birds crossed the whole Atlantic, to the seas off Newfoundland.

The team think they chased a glut of fish, then turned back to the mid-Atlantic. They ride out the winter there, at sea. Each spring, they land on the rock again.

stories.title: The Quiet Man in Cong
stories.hook: The Quiet Man's Innisfree was really Cong, Mayo.
stories.summary: The Quiet Man's Innisfree was really Cong, Mayo. In June 1951, John Ford began filming in Cong with John Wayne.
stories.body:
In June 1951, John Ford began filming in Cong with John Wayne. Ford was born in Maine, but his father had emigrated from Spiddal, Co Galway.

Maureen O'Hara, from Ranelagh in Dublin, had been offered the lead years earlier. The stars and many of the crew stayed at Ashford Castle. Local people worked as extras.

It won two Oscars: Best Colour Cinematography, and Ford's fourth for Best Director. But Cong's story is far older. Its abbey dates back to the 1100s. Long before Hollywood, Rory O'Connor, often called Ireland's last High King, retired here.

stories.title: Rathlin Island
stories.hook: Rathlin's famous spider turned up 500 years late.
stories.summary: Rathlin's famous spider turned up 500 years late. Robert the Bruce was a king on the run in 1306.
stories.body:
Robert the Bruce was a king on the run in 1306. A poem from about 70 years later sails him to Rathlin, off Antrim.

It never mentions a spider. Scott printed that, five centuries after Bruce. Scott wrote that Bruce lay in a Rathlin cabin, watching a spider.

Six times it swung for a beam and failed. So had Bruce, in six battles. On the seventh try, the thread held. So Bruce went back to fight.

Scott said a cabin. Local legend says Bruce's Cave. Scott's source was Bruce family tradition. He met Bruces who would never kill a spider.

stories.title: Reginald's Tower
stories.hook: This Waterford tower kept a Viking's name.
stories.summary: This Waterford tower kept a Viking's name. Vikings founded Waterford, with a wooden fort at its tip.
stories.body:
Vikings founded Waterford, with a wooden fort at its tip. The site carried a Norse ruler's name, Ragnall, or Reginald. Historians differ on which.

But in 1170, Strongbow's army broke through the walls. Gerald of Wales, chronicler of the conquest, already called it Reginald's tower.

He wrote that the town's leaders were seized there. The Normans later rebuilt the tower in stone, on the Viking fort.

Centuries later, an order to strike coins there still named Reginald's Tower. Through prison years and gunpowder years, the name held. Rulers changed for 800 years. The tower kept the Viking's name.

stories.title: Robert Boyle of Lismore
stories.hook: Air has a spring, said a Waterford man.
stories.summary: Air has a spring, said a Waterford man. Robert Boyle, the Earl of Cork's youngest son, was born at Lismore in 1627.
stories.body:
Robert Boyle, the Earl of Cork's youngest son, was born at Lismore in 1627. At Oxford, his assistant Robert Hooke built him an air pump.

With it, Boyle argued that air has a spring: it pushes back when squeezed. His book of 1660 put that spring on its title page.

But how strong was the spring? Two years later, he published tests on trapped air. Double the squeeze, and the air shrank to half.

Boyle credited the rule to another man, calling it Mr Towneley's hypothesis. Yet the spring of the air became Boyle's law.

stories.title: Rock of Cashel
stories.hook: Legend says the Devil spat out this rock.
stories.summary: Legend says the Devil spat out this rock. The story goes he bit it off a mountain in Co Tipperary, the Devil's Bit. Then he spat it out at Cashel, over 30 km south.
stories.body:
The story goes he bit it off a mountain in Co Tipperary, the Devil's Bit. Then he spat it out at Cashel, over 30 km south. But the rocks don't match. The Devil's Bit is sandstone, and the Rock is limestone.

Geologists say the limestone is tens of millions of years younger. Up here sat the kings of Munster. In 1101, the king gave the Rock to the Church.

In 1134, King Cormac's new chapel was consecrated here. Its wall paintings are the earliest known of their kind in Ireland. The twist? The chapel is sandstone, brought in by its builders, not the Devil.

stories.title: Rock of Dunamase
stories.hook: This rock in Laois was a dowry, twice.
stories.summary: This rock in Laois was a dowry, twice. The Rock of Dunamase was a fort of the Laois kings. The annals say Vikings plundered it.
stories.body:
The Rock of Dunamase was a fort of the Laois kings. The annals say Vikings plundered it. But in 1170, it changed hands by marriage. The King of Leinster's daughter, Aoife, wed Strongbow.

The rock went with her, and again when her daughter Isabel wed William Marshal. In Norman hands, the rock became one of Ireland's great castles.

For centuries after, Irish and English fought over it. Its end came in 1650. An old book of antiquities says it surrendered to two Cromwellian colonels. Two brides carried the rock into marriage. Two colonels, it says, took it apart.

stories.title: Ross Castle, Killarney
stories.hook: They said only a ship could take Ross.
stories.summary: They said only a ship could take Ross. Ross Castle sits on Lough Leane, near Killarney, an O'Donoghue Mór stronghold.
stories.body:
Ross Castle sits on Lough Leane, near Killarney, an O'Donoghue Mór stronghold. Its defenders, a later history says, trusted a prophecy. Ross would hold until a ship sailed the lake.

By 1652, Ross was the last Munster stronghold holding out against Cromwell. Edmund Ludlow came with about six thousand men. But water and bog ringed the castle.

So boats came by sea, and were hauled inland by hand. Ludlow wrote that each could carry 120 men. He had one rowed around the lake.

The garrison saw the boat, and asked for terms. Tradition says that boat was the ship of the prophecy.

stories.title: The Rotunda Hospital
stories.hook: Pleasure gardens helped pay for this hospital.
stories.summary: Pleasure gardens helped pay for this hospital. In 1745, surgeon Bartholomew Mosse opened a hospital for poor mothers. It was in a former theatre.
stories.body:
In 1745, surgeon Bartholomew Mosse opened a hospital for poor mothers. It was in a former theatre. In 1748, he leased land for pleasure gardens. Concerts there raised money for a bigger hospital.

Richard Cassels designed the new building. It opened on 8 December 1757. In the 1760s, a round assembly room rose next door. It gave the hospital its name, and later became the Ambassador cinema.

In the 1780s, many newborns here died within days. A doctor blamed poor ventilation, so holes were bored in the ward doors. It has served mothers and babies without a break since 1745. Today, it is called the world's oldest maternity hospital still running.

stories.title: Ireland's round towers
stories.hook: This Galway tower's door sits 8 metres up.
stories.summary: This Galway tower's door sits 8 metres up. At Kilmacduagh, George Petrie recorded that doorway in 1845. Why so high?
stories.body:
At Kilmacduagh, George Petrie recorded that doorway in 1845. Why so high? Earlier writers guessed fire temples, observatories, even Phoenician builders.

Petrie read the old annals. They call a tower cloigtheach, the bell house. So, he argued, they were Christian belfries. The high door made them refuges too.

Monks could climb in with relics and books when raiders came. But the annals record the cost. At Slane, raiders burned the bell house.

The Four Masters say it burned “with its full of reliques and good people.” A door 8 metres up might keep raiders out. It could not keep out fire.

stories.title: Royal Hospital Kilmainham
stories.hook: Dublin's first large classical building housed old soldiers.
stories.summary: Dublin's first large classical building housed old soldiers. The Duke of Ormonde laid its foundation stone in 1680. It was finished four years later.
stories.body:
The Duke of Ormonde laid its foundation stone in 1680. It was finished four years later. It followed the example of Les Invalides in Paris. That was Louis the Fourteenth's new home for army pensioners.

Its chapel has been called the finest surviving 17th-century interior in Ireland. Old soldiers lived here until 1927. It later served as Garda headquarters, then fell into disrepair.

In 1980, the government approved its restoration. The work took four years, as long as the original build. Since 1991, it has been home to the Irish Museum of Modern Art.

stories.title: The Salmon of Knowledge
stories.hook: Legend says a burnt thumb made Fionn wise.
stories.summary: Legend says a burnt thumb made Fionn wise. The tale begins at a deep pool on the Boyne, near Slane in Meath.
stories.body:
The tale begins at a deep pool on the Boyne, near Slane in Meath. There, the poet Finegas watched one salmon for seven years.

A prophecy said he would eat it, and know all things. When he caught it, his pupil Deimne had to cook it, and eat none.

Turning the spit, he burnt his thumb, and put it to his mouth. Finegas saw the boy's face had changed, and asked his name.

Deimne, said the boy. Your name is Fionn, said the poet, so the prophecy meant you. Ever after, the tale says, Fionn put that thumb to his mouth to know.

stories.title: The Sam Maguire Cup
stories.hook: Sam Maguire never won an All-Ireland medal.
stories.summary: Sam Maguire never won an All-Ireland medal. His family farmed near Dunmanway, in County Cork.
stories.body:
His family farmed near Dunmanway, in County Cork. He left the farm to be a Post Office sorter in London.

On the pitch, he reached at least three All-Ireland finals with London. London won none of them.

Off the pitch, he joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood. Many accounts say he swore in a young Michael Collins.

After Collins was killed, Sam lost his civil service job. He came home to Dunmanway, almost penniless.

Tuberculosis killed him there in 1927. So his friends gave the GAA a cup in his name. He never won the medal. Every All-Ireland football champion since has won Sam.

stories.title: Samhain & carved turnips
stories.hook: Before pumpkins, Irish kids carved turnips.
stories.summary: Before pumpkins, Irish kids carved turnips. Halloween has roots in Samhain, the Gaelic feast that began winter.
stories.body:
Halloween has roots in Samhain, the Gaelic feast that began winter. People believed the dead roamed that night. Children hollowed turnips into scary lanterns, a candle inside.

In 1943, a teacher near Fintown, Co Donegal, gave one to the National Museum. She said that kind was always made there around 1900. It was falling apart. Today its plaster copy, the ghost turnip, is on show in Co Mayo.

Irish emigrants took Halloween customs to America. There, the pumpkin took over. The museum calls it an American development of an Irish tradition. So the pumpkin on your doorstep is an Irish turnip, home in disguise.

stories.title: The Bells of Shandon
stories.hook: A Cork priest loved these bells above Rome's.
stories.summary: A Cork priest loved these bells above Rome's. Francis Mahony was born in Cork, city of the Shandon tower.
stories.body:
Francis Mahony was born in Cork, city of the Shandon tower. He became a priest, fell out with his bishop, and left Cork.

In London, he took the pen name Father Prout. Under that name, he wrote a song for the bells of his childhood.

He had heard the bells of Rome and Paris, the song says. None sounded so grand as Shandon, on the pleasant waters of the Lee.

His book of 1836 carried those bells far beyond Cork. Mahony stayed abroad, and died in Paris in 1866. His body came home to Shandon, to rest within sound of his bells.

stories.title: Skellig Michael
stories.hook: Luke Skywalker's island is off Kerry.
stories.summary: Luke Skywalker's island is off Kerry. It is Skellig Michael, 12 km out in the Atlantic. Monks built a monastery here over 1,000 years ago.
stories.body:
It is Skellig Michael, 12 km out in the Atlantic. Monks built a monastery here over 1,000 years ago. Reaching it means 618 steep, uneven steps. The monks prayed and slept in beehive huts of stone.

In 1996, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In July 2014, a Star Wars crew filmed there for three days. It became the final scene of The Force Awakens.

The crew returned in 2015 for The Last Jedi. Designer Jake Lunt Davies says the island's puffins inspired the porgs. The monks left in the 1200s. Most of their huts, built without mortar, still stand.

stories.title: Slieve League cliffs
stories.hook: On Slieve League, even the guide was afraid.
stories.summary: On Slieve League, even the guide was afraid. Writer Stephen Gwynn walked up these Donegal cliffs, about 600 metres high.
stories.body:
Writer Stephen Gwynn walked up these Donegal cliffs, about 600 metres high. He went with a fisherman going up to cut turf, and took him as guide.

At Bunglass, the sea lay far below. Sunlit spray made a rainbow under them. Then came what he called One Man's Path, a stone edge about two feet across. It must be done on hands and knees, he wrote.

Gwynn called it nothing to be afraid of. Guides, he warned, try to frighten you. But Gwynn wrote that his own guide was afraid. He would not carry the writer's raincoat over, blaming bad boots.

stories.title: Sligo Rovers & the Showgrounds
stories.hook: Sligo Rovers' ground began as a farm show.
stories.summary: Sligo Rovers' ground began as a farm show. The club was founded in 1928 and has played at the Showgrounds ever since.
stories.body:
The club was founded in 1928 and has played at the Showgrounds ever since. In January 1939, it signed Dixie Dean. He once scored 60 league goals for Everton in one season.

His daughter said the mayor and a brass band met his train. He was not on it. Aged 32, he once scored five goals in one game against Waterford.

In Sligo's first FAI Cup final, on 23 April 1939, he scored. Shelbourne won the replay. In 1968, the ground was bought for the club. Today it is held in trust for the people of Sligo.

stories.title: Smock Alley Theatre
stories.hook: A theatre, a whiskey store, then a church.
stories.summary: A theatre, a whiskey store, then a church. In 1662, John Ogilby opened the Theatre Royal in Smock Alley.
stories.body:
In 1662, John Ogilby opened the Theatre Royal in Smock Alley. On 26 December 1670, the upper gallery collapsed during a play. People were killed and many were hurt.

In 1737, Dublin-born Peg Woffington played Ophelia here. She went on to become a star in London. In 1754, a political row over a play sparked a riot. The angry crowd wrecked the theatre's interior.

The theatre closed in 1787. It became a whiskey warehouse, then a Catholic church from 1811. In 2012, it reopened as a restored theatre, 350 years after it first opened. Today it is Dublin's municipal theatre.

stories.title: Spike Island, Cork
stories.hook: A Cork fort took one prisoner's name.
stories.summary: A Cork fort took one prisoner's name. Fort Westmoreland sits atop Spike Island in Cork Harbour.
stories.body:
Fort Westmoreland sits atop Spike Island in Cork Harbour. In 1847, as the Famine spread, the fort became a convict prison.

Eight months later, a navy ship brought John Mitchel, a Young Ireland writer. From the deck, he called Spike Island "a rueful looking place".

After four nights in a vaulted cell, a warship took him to Bermuda. Behind him, the prison filled. About 1,200 convicts died there.

After the Treaty, Britain kept the fort. In 1938, the Irish army took it over. Years later, it took the name of a man held there four nights: Fort Mitchel.

stories.title: St. Brendan's voyage
stories.hook: A leather boat sailed from Kerry to Newfoundland.
stories.summary: A leather boat sailed from Kerry to Newfoundland. It was built to test the story of St Brendan, a 6th-century monk born in Kerry.
stories.body:
It was built to test the story of St Brendan, a 6th-century monk born in Kerry. Centuries later, a Latin tale, the Navigatio, told of his seven-year voyage with monks.

In one scene, his monks light a fire on an island that starts to move. It is a whale. Could a boat like his cross the Atlantic? In 1976, Tim Severin sailed one of oak, ash and ox hide to find out.

It left Brandon Creek near Dingle and, via Iceland, reached Newfoundland in June 1977. It proved the voyage could be done. Whether Brendan did it is still not proven.

stories.title: St. Brigid's Cross
stories.hook: Legend says this cross began as floor rushes.
stories.summary: Legend says this cross began as floor rushes. Brigid of Kildare, the story goes, sat by a dying chieftain's bed.
stories.body:
Brigid of Kildare, the story goes, sat by a dying chieftain's bed. She wove floor rushes into a cross and told him what it meant. He asked to be baptised.

Her feast, the first of February, falls on Imbolc, the old start of spring. That day, families hung new crosses over the door. Brigid, people believed, would bless and protect the house.

Over a century ago, a Kildare journal drew one, woven of straw. Such a straw cross stayed up indoors a full year, till a new one replaced it. In many homes, last year's cross comes down, and fresh rushes go up.

stories.title: St. Patrick's Cathedral
stories.hook: This cathedral's Dean wrote Gulliver's Travels.
stories.summary: This cathedral's Dean wrote Gulliver's Travels. Jonathan Swift was its Dean from 1713 to 1745.
stories.body:
Jonathan Swift was its Dean from 1713 to 1745. He was buried here, beside his friend Stella, as he wished.

He left most of his fortune to found a hospital for the mentally ill. It still exists. Oliver Cromwell once stabled his horses in its nave.

In 1492, two feuding families made peace by shaking hands through a hole in a door here. Legend says that gave us "chancing your arm". It is Ireland's largest church, and unusually, not the seat of a bishop.

stories.title: The first St. Patrick's Day parade
stories.hook: The first recorded St Patrick's parade? Not Ireland.
stories.summary: The first recorded St Patrick's parade? Not Ireland. St Augustine, Florida. Spanish records found by historian Michael Francis suggest a procession in 1601.
stories.body:
St Augustine, Florida. Spanish records found by historian Michael Francis suggest a procession in 1601. Cannons fired from the fort as they passed. The town's Irish priest, Ricardo Artur, likely started it.

In 1762, Irish soldiers serving in the British Army marched through New York. Irish societies kept it going. In 1909, Kerrymen marched behind a banner of Daniel O'Connell.

At home, St Patrick's Day only became a bank holiday in 1903. The parade began with the Irish who left. Then it came home.

stories.title: St. Stephen's Green
stories.hook: Gunfire here reportedly paused for ducks.
stories.summary: Gunfire here reportedly paused for ducks. Until 1663, St Stephen's Green was a marshy common.
stories.body:
Until 1663, St Stephen's Green was a marshy common. It was walled in. Only wealthy neighbours could use it.

In 1877, a law was passed to reopen it to the public. Sir Arthur Guinness, later Lord Ardilaun, pushed for it. He paid for a new layout. The gates reopened in July 1880.

In 1916, rebels dug in here. British troops in the Shelbourne Hotel could fire on them. Reports say both sides held fire so the park keeper could feed the ducks.

stories.title: The Strawberry Beds
stories.hook: Dublin has a riverbank named after strawberries.
stories.summary: Dublin has a riverbank named after strawberries. The Strawberry Beds is the Liffey's steep north bank, west of the Phoenix Park. Its sheltered, south-facing slopes grew strawberries for generations.
stories.body:
The Strawberry Beds is the Liffey's steep north bank, west of the Phoenix Park. Its sheltered, south-facing slopes grew strawberries for generations. In 1835, the Dublin Penny Journal said parties of pleasure came at fruit time.

It called the river drive through the Beds to Lucan the citizens' favourite. Horse-drawn cars ran from Carlisle Bridge, now O'Connell Bridge, at 3d a seat.

On fine Sundays, a line of cars stretched from Parkgate Street to Knockmaroon. An 1895 guide said strawberries and cream could be had there. Locals recall them served on a cabbage leaf.

stories.title: The 1924 Tailteann Games
stories.hook: Olympic champions raced in a Dublin Zoo pond.
stories.summary: Olympic champions raced in a Dublin Zoo pond. It was August 1924, at Ireland's Tailteann Games.
stories.body:
It was August 1924, at Ireland's Tailteann Games. The old tales placed such games at Teltown, in Meath.

One book boasted they were older than the Greek Olympics. Soon after the Civil War, the new Free State revived them.

Held after the Paris Olympics, they drew stars like American Johnny Weissmuller. But Ireland had no pool good enough, so they swam in a zoo pond.

The games ran twice more, then faded after 1932. The story of the pond did not. Weissmuller later played Tarzan, lord of the jungle. One Irish writer called the zoo an uncannily prescient venue.

stories.title: The Ark of the Covenant at Tara
stories.hook: They dug into Tara to find the Ark.
stories.summary: They dug into Tara to find the Ark. The diggers were British-Israelites. They believed Anglo-Saxons descended from ancient Israel.
stories.body:
The diggers were British-Israelites. They believed Anglo-Saxons descended from ancient Israel. They were sure the Ark of the Covenant lay under Tara.

In 1899, with the landlord's permission, they dug into the Rath of the Synods. The digging destroyed much of the rath's shape.

By 1902, Douglas Hyde, W. B. Yeats and George Moore protested in The Times. Their letter called Tara probably the most consecrated spot in Ireland.

Then Maud Gonne brought hundreds of children there in protest. After three years, the protests halted the dig. The diggers found Roman coins. Of the Ark, not a trace.

stories.title: Temple Bar
stories.hook: Temple Bar was almost a bus station.
stories.summary: Temple Bar was almost a bus station. The name likely comes from the Temple family. Sir William Temple built a house and gardens here in the early 1600s.
stories.body:
The name likely comes from the Temple family. Sir William Temple built a house and gardens here in the early 1600s. The street name first appears on a map in 1673.

Centuries later, the state transport company planned to knock it down for a bus terminus. Meanwhile, it rented the buildings out cheaply. Artists and galleries moved in.

Protests stopped the plan. In 1991, the government set up Temple Bar Properties to regenerate it. Today, it's Dublin's cultural quarter.

stories.title: Thomas Francis Meagher & the Tricolour
stories.hook: Ireland's flag holds a peace he never saw.
stories.summary: Ireland's flag holds a peace he never saw. Thomas Francis Meagher first flew it on Waterford's Mall in March 1848.
stories.body:
Thomas Francis Meagher first flew it on Waterford's Mall in March 1848. Its white, he said, meant a lasting truce between Orange and Green.

But that summer's rising failed. Sentenced to death, he was shipped to Van Diemen's Land. He escaped to New York, and raised the Irish Brigade in the civil war.

At Fredericksburg, the brigade charged a stone wall. Hundreds of its men fell. Peace made him Montana's acting governor. At Fort Benton in 1867, accounts say he fell from a steamboat.

His body was never found. The Constitution makes the tricolour Ireland's flag. His truce still waits in white.

stories.title: Tom Crean, Antarctic explorer
stories.hook: A Kerryman walked 18 hours alone for help.
stories.summary: A Kerryman walked 18 hours alone for help. In 1912, Tom Crean from Annascaul was on Scott's South Pole expedition.
stories.body:
In 1912, Tom Crean from Annascaul was on Scott's South Pole expedition. Lieutenant Teddy Evans got scurvy. Crean and William Lashly hauled him on a sledge.

About 35 miles from Hut Point, they could go no further. Crean went on alone. After 18 hours, he reached help. Teddy Evans lived, and both men won the Albert Medal.

Scott's polar party, Edgar Evans among them, never came back. In 1916, he went for help again, 17 days in a small boat with Shackleton. Back in Annascaul, he opened the South Pole Inn. He rarely spoke of the ice again.

stories.title: How 'Tory' came from Ireland
stories.hook: Britain's Tories took their name from Irish outlaws.
stories.summary: Britain's Tories took their name from Irish outlaws. Stripped of his family's land in Armagh, Redmond O'Hanlon took to the hills.
stories.body:
Stripped of his family's land in Armagh, Redmond O'Hanlon took to the hills. Men like him were called tóruidhe. One Irish dictionary says: a pursued person.

Dublin pursued him by name, offering a hundred pounds, dead or alive. Still he held out for years, as Count Hanlon.

Meanwhile, London split over whether James, a Catholic, should be king. James's opponents mocked his backers as tories: Irish outlaws.

Then, in April 1681, accounts say, O'Hanlon's own foster-brother shot him dead. That year the insult stuck, and its targets took it as their name. Britain's Conservatives still answer to the outlaws' name.

stories.title: Limerick's Treaty Stone
stories.hook: Limerick's Treaty Stone is half its old size.
stories.summary: Limerick's Treaty Stone is half its old size. Beside Thomond Bridge, it was once a step for mounting horses.
stories.body:
Beside Thomond Bridge, it was once a step for mounting horses. Tradition says the Treaty of Limerick was signed on it, in 1691.

The treaty ended the Williamite war. It promised Catholics freedom to practise their faith. But the Irish Parliament ratified only a cut-down version. Penal laws followed.

So Limerick came to be called the City of the Broken Treaty. The story made the stone famous. Visitors chipped off pieces to carry home.

To stop them, the city raised it onto a pedestal in 1865. About half the stone remains. Its pedestal still reads: The Treaty of Limerick, signed.
