stories.title: The Tribes of Galway
stories.hook: Galway's nickname, they say, began as an insult.
stories.summary: Galway's nickname, they say, began as an insult. Fourteen merchant families ran the walled town of Galway for centuries.
stories.body:
Fourteen merchant families ran the walled town of Galway for centuries. They traded across Europe and married into each other's families. Above one doorway, the Browne and Lynch coats of arms sit side by side.

Then, in 1652, Cromwell's army took Galway after a long siege. Its soldiers, the story goes, mocked how the families stuck together. They called them the tribes of Galway.

The historian James Hardiman wrote that story down in 1820. He said the families took up the name with pride. So the insult became a badge. Galway still calls itself the City of the Tribes.

stories.title: Trim Castle
stories.hook: Meath's great castle began as a burned house.
stories.summary: Meath's great castle began as a burned house. King Henry II gave Meath to Hugh de Lacy in 1172.
stories.body:
King Henry II gave Meath to Hugh de Lacy in 1172. He fortified a house at Trim, with a trench and a stockade.

Then he sailed for England and left Hugh Tyrrell in charge. But the High King, Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, marched on Trim.

Tyrrell had too few men, and fled. The house went up in flames. So de Lacy began again, in stone.

In 1186, he went to view a new castle at Durrow. A youth from Teffia drew an axe and killed him, the annals say. His son finished the keep. Where the house burned, the stone still stands.

stories.title: Trinity College Dublin
stories.hook: Catholic bishops barred Catholics from here until 1970.
stories.summary: Catholic bishops barred Catholics from here until 1970. This rule, with few exceptions, began in 1871.
stories.body:
This rule, with few exceptions, began in 1871. Queen Elizabeth the First founded it by royal charter in 1592. It is Ireland's oldest university.

Its Long Room was built between 1712 and 1732. It housed 200,000 of the library's oldest books. The Campanile was finished in 1854. Its Great Bell tolls before exams.

Women were admitted as full members for the first time in 1904. Former students include Oscar Wilde, Jonathan Swift, Bram Stoker and Samuel Beckett.

stories.title: The Valentia transatlantic cable
stories.hook: The first transatlantic telegram went through Kerry.
stories.summary: The first transatlantic telegram went through Kerry. In August 1858, a cable linked Valentia Island to Newfoundland. Queen Victoria cabled the US President.
stories.body:
In August 1858, a cable linked Valentia Island to Newfoundland. Queen Victoria cabled the US President. Reports say her 98 words took about 16 hours. It was complete at five the next morning.

Within weeks, the line went dead. Too much voltage, meant to speed it up, helped ruin it. In 1866, the Great Eastern laid a new cable from Valentia. It was the biggest ship afloat.

On 27 July, it reached Heart's Content, Newfoundland. This time, it held. News that took ten days by ship now took minutes. Valentia stayed on the line for a century, until 1966.

stories.title: Viking Dublin
stories.hook: Dublin's council offices were built on Viking Dublin.
stories.summary: Dublin's council offices were built on Viking Dublin. In 841, Vikings set up a naval camp at Dubh Linn, the black pool.
stories.body:
In 841, Vikings set up a naval camp at Dubh Linn, the black pool. Viking Dublin grew into a busy trading town, by the Liffey at Wood Quay.

From 1974 to 1981, museum archaeologists dug the site. They found over 100 houses and thousands of objects. In 1978, about 20,000 people marched to Save Wood Quay. The offices went ahead.

Finds like combs and jewellery are now on show at the National Museum of Ireland. Today, part of the Viking-era city wall, from about 1100, survives inside those offices.

stories.title: The Battle of Vinegar Hill (1798)
stories.hook: The rebels escaped through a general's gap.
stories.summary: The rebels escaped through a general's gap. In 1798, Wexford rose. Rebels led by Father John Murphy took Enniscorthy.
stories.body:
In 1798, Wexford rose. Rebels led by Father John Murphy took Enniscorthy. They camped on Vinegar Hill, above the town, for over three weeks.

So General Lake came with over 13,000 men, by one count of the time. His plan was to surround the hill and trap them.

The guns opened at seven. But General Needham's column was not in place. A writer of the time says he arrived at nine, when the business was over.

So one side of the hill lay open. Most rebels fled that way, though hundreds were killed. Soon that open side had a mocking name: Needham's gap.

stories.title: Irish National War Memorial Gardens
stories.hook: This Dublin garden honours 49,400 Irish war dead.
stories.summary: This Dublin garden honours 49,400 Irish war dead. The figure comes from eight books of names, printed in 1923. Historians say it is not exact.
stories.body:
The figure comes from eight books of names, printed in 1923. Historians say it is not exact. Harry Clarke drew their borders: trenches, guns, ruins, graves and soldiers.

Edwin Lutyens designed the garden at Islandbridge, with four granite bookrooms. Work began in 1931. Half the men had served in the British Army, half in the Irish National Army.

To make jobs, they worked mostly by hand, hauling granite with poles and ropes. An opening set for 1939 was called off as war loomed. The gardens waited almost fifty years. They were formally dedicated in 1988. Their name liveth for evermore.

stories.title: William Rowan Hamilton's bridge
stories.hook: He cut his answer into a Dublin bridge.
stories.summary: He cut his answer into a Dublin bridge. For years, William Rowan Hamilton tried to multiply triples of numbers.
stories.body:
For years, William Rowan Hamilton tried to multiply triples of numbers. In October 1843, his two boys asked each morning at Dunsink:

"Well, Papa, can you multiply triplets?" "No, I can only add and subtract them." One Monday, he walked into Dublin along the Royal Canal.

At Broom Bridge, in Cabra, the answer came: four numbers, not three. With a knife, he cut the rule into the stone.

i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1. He later wrote that the carving had crumbled away. Now a stone plaque holds his answer. Each year on that day, walkers retrace his steps.

stories.title: W. B. Yeats at Drumcliffe
stories.hook: Yeats wrote his own grave in a poem.
stories.summary: Yeats wrote his own grave in a poem. It names Drumcliffe churchyard in Sligo, where his great-grandfather was rector.
stories.body:
It names Drumcliffe churchyard in Sligo, where his great-grandfather was rector. The poem even sets the words for his stone.

But he died on the French Riviera in January 1939. His wife said he asked to lie there, then be planted in Sligo.

Then the war held that up for years. So in 1948, the Irish ship Macha carried him home.

Doubts grew, but his children were sure it was him. Then French diplomatic papers suggested his bones were mixed with other remains. Either way, Sligo kept the grave he wrote: cast a cold eye on life, on death. Horseman, pass by.
